Measuring California’s Efforts to Build More Housing

A Complete Review of

California’s Housing Element Annual Progress Report (APR) Process

from Jurisdictions to the

Department of Housing and Community Development

Possibility Lab, UC Berkeley

October 2026

Read the Report Briefing ↓

This project was funded by the California Department of Housing and Community Development and the California Community Foundation as part of the Possibility Lab’s Abundance Accelerator. The contents may not necessarily reflect the official views or policies of the State of California, the California Community Foundation and its Donors, or the University of California.

California state law requires all cities and counties to submit a Housing Element Annual Progress Report (APR) to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) by April 1 each year.

The APR tracks the full housing production pipeline: project applications submitted, planning approvals, building permit approvals, and construction completion, as well as units demolished, rehabilitated, or converted.

Our findings draw from a statewide survey reaching 173 jurisdictions, as well as in-depth interviews from a stratified sample of 11 jurisdictions representing the diversity of localities within the state, and a small focus group with local California housing planners and government staff.

This report aims to support HCD in collecting high-quality housing data while reducing burdens on local governments.

As such, our study is not an assessment of APR data accuracy, but rather focused on helping local governments do the APR.

How might California’s system for accelerating and tracking housing progress look different if it were co-designed with the people involved in its implementation?

Report Briefing

California state law requires all cities and counties to submit a Housing Element Annual Progress Report (APR) to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) by April 1 each year. The APR tracks the full housing production pipeline: project applications submitted, planning approvals, building permit approvals, and construction completion, as well as units demolished, rehabilitated, or converted. As such, the housing data collected through the APR provides a uniquely comprehensive snapshot of California housing production. While other datasets like the Census Building Permit Survey (BPS) also capture robust permitting trends, the APR offers a level of detail across development milestones about unit affordability and structure type that sets it apart.

It is essential for APR data to be accurate. HCD uses APR data to assess jurisdictional compliance with local Housing Element plans, track progress toward Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) targets by income category, and identify unmet housing needs. Advocates, policymakers, and researchers rely on it to evaluate statewide housing development trends and broader housing policy impacts. Since 2018, HCD has provided the APR form as an Excel template for jurisdictions to complete and submit their annual reports. Since then, the APR form has grown every year to incorporate other legislatively mandated reporting categories, from the use of density bonuses or various streamlining laws to tracking some forms of residential rehabilitation, rezoned areas, and student housing.

In 2025, HCD partnered with the UC Berkeley Possibility Lab to examine how local jurisdictions collect, manage, and report APR data. Rather than evaluating individual jurisdictions' compliance, this study identifies structural features of the APR process that may interfere with the ability of local jurisdictions to feasibly report housing data at the level of detail required. As such, our study is not an assessment of APR data accuracy, but rather focused on helping local governments do the APR.

Our findings draw from a statewide survey reaching 173 jurisdictions, as well as in-depth interviews from a stratified sample of 11 jurisdictions representing the diversity of localities within the state, and a small focus group with local California housing planners and government staff. Data collection to inform this report was conducted in three sequential phases between March and September 2025. Importantly, the survey, interviews, and focus group are limited in that they do not directly measure the empirical accuracy of jurisdictions’ APR submissions. However, when comparing the APR data to the Census BPS data, we find similar overall trends in the number of permitted units, where the direction of annual change is consistent in each dataset.

Taken as a whole, this study underscores the logistical challenges faced by local jurisdictions when preparing the APR and integrating new reporting requirements. The manual entry required to input various data points into the APR form increases the potential for human error, making it burdensome for local planners to ensure they are reporting complete and accurate data. Moreover, various data points are not consistently documented in jurisdictions’ existing administrative processes, requiring local planners to retrospectively track down information on a project-by-project basis when preparing the APR. The planners working on the APR take steps to validate their reported data to ensure accuracy. Nonetheless, mitigating the challenges identified in our study remains essential for enabling local governments to feasibly fulfill their data reporting obligations.

This report aims to support HCD in collecting high-quality housing data while reducing burdens on local governments. Given our findings, we’ve identified a range of specific recommendations for HCD to improve the APR process for all California jurisdictions. We acknowledge that some of these interventions may not be relevant to all jurisdictions across the state due to their varying sizes, resources, and capacities, and recognize that support from HCD may be more valuable for some jurisdictions than others.

The APR in its current form is still relatively new, and it is reasonable to assume the state will continue to collect data on housing production for years to come. As such, it is worthwhile for HCD to reflect on how the process is working, to correct issues that are identified, and to redirect course as appropriate. In this briefing, we outline the recommendations we provided to HCD as a result of our research. When preparing our report, we communicated our findings to HCD staff, who began taking action to implement the study’s recommendations, as summarized by HCD staff at the end of this briefing.

While our recommendations focus on potential interventions for HCD, the findings of our study have implications for the broader policymaking process in California. Each and every reporting requirement in the APR form is mandated by state legislation. The California Legislature requires HCD to oversee local compliance with reporting obligations, but the Legislature lacks meaningful insight into whether local governments are equipped to fulfill this function. In other words, the feedback loop is broken. How might California’s system for accelerating and tracking housing progress look different if it were co-designed with the people involved in its implementation? We offer this question as food for thought to all participants in California policymaking.

Recommendations to HCD

1. Suggested Changes to HCD’s APR Team Processes

If HCD is going to hold jurisdictions accountable for inadequate APR submissions, the department should ensure it is helping set up local governments for success. Specifically, HCD should develop and provide assistance to local governments to help them track and manage housing development data that will be reported in the APR. Jurisdictions, especially those with fewer resources, would benefit from the additional support, and HCD could better equip jurisdictions to collect and report accurate data consistent with the department’s standards.

1a. Provide guidance to clarify common points of confusion

There are certain project types and unique situations that jurisdictions struggle to report in the APR and about which HCD could provide more clarity. Specifically, planners communicated that it is not clear how they should report project amendments in the APR or precisely how to handle large master-planned developments that ultimately have many housing units and multiple buildings. In both cases, planners seem to have rightfully concluded that the APR format was not set up with these circumstances in mind. HCD staff could issue guidance to jurisdictions about how best to report on these kinds of circumstances in the APR.

1b. Provide APR instructions and guidance in more and varied formats

The role of preparing the APR frequently shifts among local government staff members. More than 20% of survey respondents, all of whom worked on the 2024 APR, reported that this was the first year they had done so. HCD’s APR Instructions and Frequently Asked Questions documents are helpful to local government staff but still insufficient. By defining terms and explaining all fields in the submission form, the existing resources help users navigate the APR, which is otherwise unintuitive for many. That said, we heard from planners who identify as more visual or auditory learners that the written instructions are not the most useful to them, and several interviewees specifically mentioned that they would benefit from instructions in the form of a video.

HCD should record and post additional videos related to specific APR topics. HCD already holds information sessions and webinars about the APR, and there is demand for this content: 56% of survey respondents attended one of these events in late 2024 or early 2025. Creating additional how-to videos may have the effect of reducing the number of questions sent to the APR inbox, thus reducing staff time spent responding to individual emails.

1c. Communicate any new APR requirements at the start of the reporting year and provide technical assistance for implementation

Local governments are constantly generating data on project applications submitted, planning approvals, and building permit approvals as housing projects move through the development pipeline. This data is stored in jurisdictions’ permit tracking systems, which are often deliberately set up to be conducive for preparing the APR, such as by including fields to collect all of the required data.

When the APR form changes from year to year, local governments must adapt to meet the new requirements. Even if the changes are relatively minor, it is possible (and even likely) that local governments have not been collecting data in that format or collecting that information at all during the reporting year. Interviewees expressed frustration about being made aware of changes to the APR near the end of the reporting year, especially if the change requires them to track down pieces of information they had not been recording for projects. A late adjustment to the APR creates more work for local government staff in the few months before the APR is due, which is already a period of overwork for many of the people tasked with preparing APRs.

Ideally, jurisdictions would be informed of any changes to the APR form at least a year in advance so they can appropriately adjust their data collection and storage throughout the reporting year. As an example, this might entail modifying their local application forms so project applicants submit certain pieces of information required for the APR at the outset. Some planners we spoke with feel that they are always updating their data systems and procedures because the APR regularly changes. This is especially challenging because making systematic changes can be a slow, gradual process, and local governments may plan for them months or years in advance.

1d. Provide guidance, including “plug-and-play” templates, for the most common permit tracking software systems used by jurisdictions

Among survey respondents, 87.3% reported that their jurisdiction uses some kind of “gov tech” software to track housing projects across development milestones and collect data from applications, planning approvals, building permit approvals, and construction completion. However, many jurisdictions are extracting APR data from software systems that were not specifically designed to produce it.

Software systems designed for permit tracking can be customized to varying degrees, from modifying what fields are included and designing report templates, to integration with other systems. For completing the Housing Element APR, this means that the software collects all of the required data or exports data in a structure that is conducive for transferring to the APR submission form.

Many of the commercial permit software systems allow for some amount of customization of the fields, settings, and data exports. This includes creating “templates” for reports or exporting data from the software. As long as the APR uses a spreadsheet format, how jurisdictions transfer data from their permit software to a spreadsheet format will remain a significant part of the APR preparation process. Some jurisdictions have identified “translating” their data into the APR format as a roadblock in the process and have adjusted their permit software to the extent possible, designing templates that include the specific pieces of information required for the APR and in a similar format.

Currently, jurisdictions must all individually prepare these templates and figure out the customization settings on their own, but HCD could ease the burden on local governments by providing guidance or even developing templates themselves for the most common software systems identified in our survey.

1e. Clearly establish the goals and purpose of the APR, especially as HCD’s authority for overseeing the process grows

Through interviews and our focus group, it became clear that many planners who work on the APR are not aware of or misunderstand why every city and county in California is required to complete the APR. Comments from several planners suggested they view the APR as something HCD simply forces them to do, without realizing that the requirements are legislatively mandated or that the data provide uniquely comprehensive insights into housing development across the state in a way that no other publicly accessible dataset does. This misunderstanding may lead some local staff to question the necessity of certain details — highlighting the importance of clear guidance to support consistent and confident reporting. Planners who are less aware of the APR’s goals and purposes may not view the APR as important to their work and thus be less intrinsically motivated to work on it.

In all of its messaging about the APR, HCD should include a brief explanation of why local governments must collect and submit housing production data each year. This could include a brief overview of the history and goals of the APR at the beginning of videos and webinars, as well as in written instructions or guides to preparing the APR. HCD might also explain why the accuracy of specific data points is important for policymaking or evaluation.

Particularly as HCD explores its expanded authority to reject APRs that do not substantially meet requirements through Assembly Bill (AB) 2653 (Chapter 657, Statutes of 2022), HCD could develop new technical assistance materials, such as review standards for the APR form and process, to help jurisdictions clearly understand why they may be subject to additional scrutiny when an APR is rejected or when HCD asks for revisions after submission.1

2. Suggested Changes to the APR Form

One finding that arose from nearly all of our interviews and in many survey responses is that the Microsoft Excel APR submission form is challenging to use. When asked about the biggest challenges to submitting complete and accurate APR data, the most common response was the design of the APR submission form itself, which 21% of survey respondents mentioned unprompted.

2a. Change elements of the APR submission form to make it easier to input data

Planners expressed frustration that there are built-in limitations on what users can do, such as not being able to filter data, sort columns, or copy-and-paste rows of data. Making systematic changes to the APR form that allow for more flexibility is within HCD’s “form authority” and has the potential to save significant staff time.2 A revised form might lift some of the less necessary programmed limitations or macros, such as by allowing users to paste rows of data into the tables. This change could limit frustration and reduce the amount of time planners spend working on data entry for the APR. One interviewee memorably described their experience “fighting with the macros.” Given the challenges reported in our data, HCD might consider reassessing if the negative impacts of programmed elements outweigh the intended benefits.

We also acknowledge that HCD has taken measures to make the APR form easier for local government staff to use and complete. Specifically, the workbook is programmed to automatically run most calculations and to auto-populate some fields and tables. These components of the workbook’s programming help ease the burden on planners and may reduce the amount of time spent preparing the APR submission.

2b. Consider alternative formats for collecting project-level data across development milestones

Interview and focus group participants described difficulties linking data when completing Table A2 of the APR form, where jurisdictions report on planning approvals, building permit approvals, and construction completion. Planners from large jurisdictions said linking this data was one of the most time-consuming and tedious parts of the APR. Given this, HCD might consider alternative formats for collecting project-level data across development milestones.

Though the APR submission form has been constructed to include fields for all of the required information and is intended to be suitable for most projects, interviewees felt that the current system is still not well-suited to reporting certain kinds of information. In particular, interviewees note that the current APR form is not set up to easily track large developments that begin with one large lot and result in hundreds or even thousands of new housing units across multiple subdivisions. These “family-tree” developments can be more difficult to report in the APR, as compared to those that follow a more linear project pathway.

Likewise, a few interviewees reported that it can be difficult to document project amendments in the APR form. Some planners worried about incorrectly reporting units twice (“double-dipping”) or confusing the development timeline when they needed to report a project amendment, such as its number of units or the composition of units by income level. Notably, HCD staff who work on APRs have similarly mentioned that there are instances when it is unclear how jurisdictions should report certain kinds of amendments to project milestones that have already been reported in a previous APR.3

Interviewees described how tracking a project as it moves through the development pipeline—by linking the project’s planning approvals, building permits, and construction completion—can create opportunities for errors or duplicates to emerge in Table A2. Compounding this challenge, projects often reach these milestones in different years and thus should appear in multiple years’ APRs, potentially making it more difficult to identify errors.

3. Suggested Changes to the Broader APR Process

3a. Require and support a shift toward assigning unique project identifiers

Linking project-level data across development milestones is one of the most persistent challenges planners face. In some cases, jurisdictions may not consistently assign a unique identifier to a given project as it progresses through the development phases, which can obscure linkages between project data across different documentation sources. Our findings suggest that the underlying documentation processes are a potential root cause of the difficulties faced when collecting and reporting accurate APR data, particularly for Tables A and A2.

One of the potential benefits of technology solutions is to more easily enable linking of all records for the same project, but tech solutions are only as good as their underlying documentation sources. Hypothetically, a unique project identifier could be reported in the APR as the “Local Jurisdiction Tracking ID,” thus resolving the shortcomings of APNs for linking project-level data across milestones. By our own observation, though, the local application materials used by jurisdictions in their development processes do not consistently assign each project a unique project identifier that is recorded across each development milestone.

For jurisdictions that do not yet have this, HCD might work with local staff to set up a system where every project has a unique project identifier that is generated when an application is received and then attached to the project until its completion, which could make it easier for local government staff to track projects over time. If pursued, this intervention would be most effective if overseen by internal HCD staff (rather than consultants) to ensure alignment with existing systems and continued support moving forward. While likely requiring substantial resources and time on the part of HCD, this intervention could nonetheless help address the challenges that local staff face when preparing the APR via the existing submission method, thus potentially mitigating wholesale changes to the Excel form and reducing the need for APR staff capacity to troubleshoot form challenges.

3b. Improve primary source documentation of affordability data for deed-restricted units

Assigning unique project identifiers could help ensure robust linkages between development milestones. However, in light of the APR requirements in Tables A and A2 for reporting unit-level affordability, it would also be helpful if a jurisdiction’s primary source documentation consistently recorded information about affordability, particularly for deed-restricted units where affordability commitments are typically formalized prior to the issuance of the building permit (if not before).

To support jurisdictions, HCD could offer templates for primary source materials (e.g., sample application forms) that jurisdictions could modify and adapt to their unique context, thus easing the burden of form design on jurisdictions and providing a clear course of action for planners pursuing this kind of improvement. If pursuing this kind of intervention, HCD should keep in mind the variation across jurisdictions, and potentially develop a suite of application material templates that would be appropriate for different configurations of local governance.

For example, HCD might provide one package that would be useful in jurisdictions where legal milestones (e.g., deed restrictions formalizing affordability commitments) and development milestones (e.g., the issuance of building permits) are overseen by different departments, and another package that would be sufficient where the governance of legal and development milestones is less fragmented. By incorporating these features into their primary source documentation across the project lifecycle, jurisdictions would be better positioned to continuously update their tracking systems with relevant APR information in real-time, as both legal and development milestones are administered.

While this intervention would likewise require effort on the part of internal HCD staff to accomplish (rather than consultants), the long-term benefits of improving on-the-ground data collection practices through consistent documentation of unit-level affordability data may be worth the initial investment of time and resources.

3c. Provide guidance and training related to affordability determinations for non-deed-restricted units

The two types of affordable housing units reported on in the APR—deed-restricted and non-deed restricted—have different challenges in terms of collecting and reporting data. Collecting affordability data for non-deed-restricted units is inherently difficult prior to construction completion, as rent levels remain responsive to market conditions that can fluctuate throughout the development lifecycle.

Throughout the housing development process, planning departments are not always aware of the price at which completed units are being rented or sold. HCD requires jurisdictions to report units without a deed restriction as above moderate-income, unless the jurisdiction provides an affordability justification as part of their APR submission.

While many jurisdictions in California can reasonably assume that any new, non-deed-restricted housing is affordable only to above moderate-income households, some smaller, more rural jurisdictions could potentially have new units on the market with rental or sales prices affordable to moderate-income households or below. Identifying non-deed-restricted (naturally occurring) affordable housing units for the APR is an additional burden on local government staff in the jurisdictions where that kind of housing exists, particularly for jurisdictions with non-deed-restricted housing that is affordable to lower-income households. A jurisdiction’s determination for streamlined ministerial approval under SB 423 (Chapter 778, Statutes of 2023) is based on its lower-income RHNA progress and its overall RHNA progress. In order to provide accurate APR data and receive credit toward their lower-income RHNA goals, those jurisdictions may be obligated to do additional fact-finding; however, absent an affordability justification, jurisdictions can always report new non-deed-restricted units as affordable to households with above moderate-incomes, which count toward overall RHNA progress.

Because developers are not typically obligated to lock in or report final rent levels for these units to local governments, APR reporting for this category relies heavily on estimation. Given that such data is often derived from observable characteristics (such as unit size and market location), this raises the possibility that HCD could estimate these values centrally, or at least provide more in-depth resources and guidance to help jurisdictions easily make those estimations on their own.

3d. Consider collecting APR data through updated technological approaches

The potential value of HCD changing the APR submission method is likely dependent on resolving observed challenges regarding on-the-ground data collection practices. Nonetheless, 19 planners in our study expressed a desire for a web- or cloud-based system to submit APR data more directly and easily. One potential approach could involve a streamlined submission method using an application programming interface (API) that integrates with multiple different permitting software programs to pull APR data directly from jurisdictions’ existing permit tracking systems. Transitioning to a new system along these lines could be a multi-year process that requires significant investment and coordination, so this recommendation should be considered as a long-term goal.

If pursued, these changes could meaningfully streamline the APR process across the board. However, if the data collection challenges observed in our study are not resolved, then the greater ease enabled by alternative methods for APR submission will only partially mitigate the level of burden placed on local jurisdictions to report accurate data.

If pursuing alternative submission models, HCD should also anticipate associated limitations, especially for low-capacity jurisdictions that lack capable software systems and have minimal ability to procure them. Yet while alternative methods for APR submission would not necessarily benefit jurisdictions with limited capacity for software improvements, HCD could still incorporate alternative methods, such that jurisdictions have multiple options for how they submit their APRs. Higher capacity jurisdictions could take advantage of an alternative submission model, while lower capacity jurisdictions could continue submitting via an APR form.

HCD Actions Pursuant to the Recommendations

When preparing this report, the Possibility Lab communicated our findings to HCD staff, who began taking action to implement the study’s recommendations, as summarized by HCD staff below.

Actions Already Implemented

  • Recommendation 1b

    • To respond to this recommendation, HCD supplemented its guidance offered through instructional documents, APR webinars, and regular 1-on-1 technical assistance to jurisdictions. The department also created new monthly office hours, open to all planning staff working on APRs. Three office hours sessions were attended by over 100 jurisdiction staff members and were met with positive feedback.

  • Recommendation 1c

    • In accordance with this desire for advanced communication about new legislative reporting requirements being added to the APR in the upcoming reporting year, HCD has sent out an advisory memo in advance of the release of 2026 APR form materials detailing what information is needed to complete the new requirements of the upcoming form. This advanced memo in 2026 will be released even earlier in future reporting years and will be designed to provide jurisdictions more time prior to reporting to understand and compile any new data that is needed for inclusion on the upcoming APR.

  • Recommendation 1e

    • Throughout the 2025 APR reporting period, HCD prioritized communication of the ultimate goals and importance of reporting high-quality APR data through its webinars, e-blasts, and individualized technical assistance communications with jurisdictions. These communications included (1) highlighting the value of APRs as critical components of a unique statewide housing dataset that facilitates opportunities for all stakeholders to study and understand the state of housing in California, as well as (2) emphasizing the administrative use of APR data by the State to determine designations for the Streamlined Ministerial Approval Process program (SMAP) and track progress toward Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA) goals.

Actions In Progress

  • Recommendation 1b

    • Moving into the 2026 APR reporting period, HCD is in the process of developing a series of short instructional videos for planners that will provide further targeted guidance on both the introductory and complex topics critical to APR reporting. Among the many topics covered in these videos will be more clear guidance on how to report the family tree-style projects mentioned by planners and covered in recommendation 1a of the report.

  • Recommendation 1d

    • HCD’s APR team has engaged in preliminary discussions with the department’s Information Technology Branch about the possibility of developing templates for converting permitting data from commonly used software systems into a format which can be processed for the APR.

  • Recommendation 2a

    • For the 2026 reporting year, HCD will add filtering and sorting functions into the form – especially on the denser data tables like Table A and A2 – to increase the usability of the form and the ease with which jurisdictions can enter and keep track of their data.

    • HCD will also update its instructional documents and create an instructional video to better clarify how jurisdictions may copy and paste cells or freeze columns and rows in the form to fit their needs.

  • Recommendation 3c

    • HCD is working to address the challenges jurisdictions currently face in reporting the affordability of non-deed-restricted developments on the APR prior to the 2026 reporting period. HCD is working to provide (1) more clear guidance around what data and methods are required to justify a non-deed-restricted unit as affordable to moderate- or lower-income households, and (2) more resources for jurisdictions to use to help gather this required data.

  • Recommendation 3d

    • HCD also sees the benefits of migrating the APR data collection process to an integrated web form and has begun preliminary discussions with its IT Branch to outline what this transition would require over the coming years.

Background

Local housing is enshrined in state law as a matter of “vital statewide importance.” In fact, in 2017, California’s Legislature reaffirmed its declaration that the early attainment of decent housing and a suitable living environment for every Californian is a highest-order priority.4 The Legislature also affirmed that all local and state governments have a responsibility to facilitate the improvement and development of housing that provides for the housing needs of all economic segments of the community.5

California’s housing crisis has been growing since the 1970s and was exacerbated by the Great Recession.6 After decades of underproduction and land use constraints, the available supply of housing is far behind the quantity needed. As a result, housing and rental costs are soaring across the state.7 In 2024, 56% of renters and 32% of homeowners in California were burdened by housing costs on which they spent over one third of their income.8 This means that millions of Californians must make hard decisions about paying for housing at the expense of other essentials: food, health care, childcare, and transportation. One in three households in the state does not earn enough money to meet their basic needs.9

Since 1969, California has required all local city and county governments to plan for an adequate number of housing units that meet residents’ affordability needs.10 Yet California still faces a major housing shortage. Myriad, historic factors have contributed to insufficient housing production across the state. These include a lack of accountability to produce sufficient housing and historically limited oversight of local governments’ progress towards statewide housing goals.

In order to hold governments more accountable toward planning for their fair share of the housing that California needs, the state performs a unique task each year that no other state attempts to such a degree: It requires its Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) to collect comprehensive housing data from each of its cities and counties every spring.

The Regional Housing Need Allocation (RHNA) Process

State law requires a rigorous and sustained effort to forecast and plan in order to build enough housing across the state, through the Regional Housing Need Allocation (RHNA, pronounced “ree-na”) process. Each jurisdiction’s projected housing needs are determined through the RHNA process. RHNA is used to assign each city and county in California their “fair share” of new housing units to plan for. These units of housing are intended to accommodate existing needs as well as projected growth in the region.11

Planning for sufficient housing at all levels of affordability for the state’s population is at the core of RHNA, but this is not the only goal. In addition, the RHNA process is also meant to further other state planning priorities related to broader climate, economic, and equity goals by planning for housing in locations close to job centers and areas of opportunity.12

Determination: Calculating the Housing Need in Each Region

To establish RHNA housing goals for each jurisdiction in California, HCD uses census and population forecast data from the California Department of Finance to determine how much housing at a variety of affordability levels is needed for each of the state’s regions.

Because this planning process occurs for all jurisdictions across the state and is coordinated by HCD, RHNA is a continuously rolling process, where each jurisdiction repeats the process every five or eight years, depending on whether the jurisdiction is affiliated with a regional planning body, known as a Council of Governments (COG). COGs consist of multiple local governments, ranging from just a few cities to nearly 200 cities and counties. The large majority of jurisdictions in California (89.6%) are members of a COG.

Source: HCD. (2024). California’s Housing Future 2040: The Next RHNA.

Allocation: Distributing the Housing Need to Cities and Counties

After HCD determines housing goals at the regional level, the COG is then responsible for developing a methodology to allocate its housing needs to each member jurisdiction. This process includes quantifying the total number of housing units, separated into income categories, to then assign to each city, town, and county within the region.

Source: Regional Housing Needs Assessments. (2022). Auditor of the State of California. https://information.auditor.ca.gov/reports/2021-125/index.html#section3

Income-level categories for the purpose of housing planning are determined by the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development (HUD). To account for variations of median income in different areas of the country, they are based on the median income in each specific area, or area median income (AMI). Additionally, California state law defines “affordable housing cost” for lower-income households as not exceeding more than 30 percent of the gross household income.13

Local Housing Elements

At its core, RHNA is about connecting regional housing needs with the local planning process and ensuring local Housing Elements work together to address regional housing challenges. To accomplish these goals, HCD’s final housing need determination must be issued to the COG at least two years before the next housing element due date.

Based on the final RHNA numbers, each local jurisdiction must create a new Housing Element, which is typically based on aspects of the previous Element. The sites in the Housing Element’s inventory must be zoned appropriately to hold all the units of housing allocated to that jurisdiction, and must be sited to create economically feasible development opportunities.16 HCD must then review each local government’s Housing Element to determine whether it complies with state law before sending written findings back to each jurisdiction. HCD’s approval of the local Housing Element is required before a local government can formally adopt its Element as part of its overall General Plan.17

Source: HCD. (2024). California’s Housing Future 2040: The Next RHNA.

RHNA Timelines and Cycles

Officially, as of 2026, California is in the 6th RHNA cycle, meaning that all of the state’s Housing Elements are currently finalized for the 6th cycle, and the measurement of building progress will continue through 2031, at the latest.

Because RHNA occurs on a rolling basis, there is always a RHNA process happening in one part of the state or another. For example, the 7th RHNA cycle formally covers 2032 – 2040 because the last COGs in the state will be completing their Housing Element planning for that time period. These COGs include Kings County Association of Governments (KCAG) and Merced Council of Governments (MCOG). Because they are the last COGs scheduled in the 7th cycle, their RHNA process does not begin until 2029. However, some jurisdictions in California have already begun the RHNA process for the 7th cycle.18

Many rural regions of the state without a COG operate on a five-year rather than an eight-year planning period, and HCD acts as a COG for the purposes of RHNA. Counties that receive their allocations directly from HCD represent just 3% of the state’s population and 10% of the state’s total jurisdictions.19 Some of these non-COG regions began their 7th cycle RHNA planning as early as 2024. These jurisdictions repeat the RHNA process every five years, so they will also begin the 8th cycle in 2029 when other COGs are still planning their housing elements for the 7th cycle. These non-COG regions include nine total counties encompassing eight total cities: Alpine, Lassen (1 city), Mariposa, Modoc (1 city), Plumas (1 city), Sierra (1 city), Tehama (3 cities), Trinity, and Tuolumne (1 city).20

Housing Element Annual Progress Reports

Since 2006, the state has required local jurisdictions to submit comprehensive progress updates on their local housing development targets and Housing Element plans to HCD in the form of Annual Progress Reports (APR).21 Through the APR, jurisdictions demonstrate their progress toward their target housing allocations as measured by the number of building permits each jurisdiction has issued for housing units at each income level.

The Housing Development Pipeline

It can take a long time for housing developments to move from an idea through to being built and open for purchase or rent. The housing development pipeline shows the process of moving from the beginning of wanting to build through to the final confirmed construction of new units. In Figure 5 below, HCD’s Housing Element Implementation and APR Data Dashboard shows the core development milestones that show progress of housing units moving through the development pipeline. These specific milestones, as shown below, refer to (1) applications for new housing projects that have been submitted to local jurisdictions, (2) housing projects that have received all required land use approvals and entitlements necessary to apply for a building permit, (3) building permits issued for all new residential units, and (4) completed units that have received a final inspection, certificate of occupancy, or equivalent final approval.

Source: Housing Element Implementation and APR Data Dashboard. California Department of Housing and Community Development. Retrieved April 2, 2026.

For the purposes of our report, we will simplify these terms for clarity. The housing development pipeline tracks the same four key milestones, which we will refer to as:

  1. Project application submittals,

  2. Planning approvals (rather than entitlements),

  3. Building permit approvals, and

  4. Construction completion (rather than certificates of occupancy).

The APR Form

All cities and counties in California are required to submit the Housing Element APR to HCD each year to report their jurisdiction’s progress implementing its Housing Element.22 The state provides a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet template with several tabs of required data to be input, which we explain in further detail in Section 1. To monitor the full housing production pipeline, this spreadsheet requires annual data on project application submittals, planning approvals, building permit approvals, and construction completion.

It is essential that the APR data be accurate, as it is used by the state to assess jurisdictions’ compliance with Housing Element law, track progress toward achieving RHNA goals, and assess communities’ remaining housing needs. Moreover, advocates, policymakers, and researchers use the APR data to understand housing production in California and to estimate and evaluate the impacts of relevant trends, events, and public policies. The APR data has the potential to be a valuable resource, given its level of detail and potential for comparison across jurisdictions.

California’s Efforts to Build More Housing and Measure Statewide Progress

Between 2017 and 2022, the California legislature passed nearly a hundred new housing laws with the goal of significantly alleviating California’s housing challenges.23 These laws touched on virtually every aspect of housing, including streamlining approvals, reforming single-family zoning, and expanding funding programs to address homelessness. Nearly 50 of these laws directly modified the Housing Element process.24

Assembly Bill (AB) 879 (Chapter 374, Statutes of 2017) required local jurisdictions to perform analyses of their own constraints on building new housing and include their findings in the local Housing Element.25 In the same year, by amending the Housing Accountability Act, Senate Bill (SB) 167 (Chapter 368, Statutes of 2017) prohibited local jurisdictions from rejecting housing development projects for very low-, low-, or moderate-income households that were consistent with the jurisdiction’s Housing Element.26 By 2018, the Legislature expanded the Housing Accountability Act to allow any housing development project that is consistent with the local Housing Element, regardless of whether the jurisdiction has officially rezoned the area for residential development or not.27

In 2019, the Legislature’s Committee on Budget added the ability for the Attorney General to take court action and impose fines against jurisdictions that have failed to adopt an approved Housing Element.28 This law also requires HCD to post a list of jurisdictions that have failed to adopt a compliant Housing Element on its website.29

For the recent rollout of the 2025 APR form and process, statutory requirements added at least one new table (Table L, 2025) to report newly listed historical designations in each jurisdiction, which also appear as new columns in two existing tables on the form (Tables A and A2).30 Clearly, the state continues to build reporting requirements onto the APR process that require additional fields of information to monitor housing development.

HCD’s Authority to Reject APRs

In September 2022, the state legislature passed AB 2653 (Chapter 657, Statutes of 2022) authorizing HCD to reject the housing element portion of an APR if the report is not in substantial compliance with legal requirements. If HCD rejects the housing element portion of an annual report, HCD must provide the reasons for the APR rejection in writing.31 Examples of reasons that might trigger a rejection include non-compliance with data standards, missing or incomplete data, and unclear justifications for reporting non-deed-restricted units as affordable. As of 2026, HCD has been in a multi-year effort to develop systems for ensuring consistent practices when exercising this authority. In order to effectively leverage this enforcement authority, and more broadly to improve the overall quality of APR data, HCD has sought to become more familiar with local governments’ data collection processes from which many APR errors may stem. This report is part of that effort.

Research Methodology

In 2025, the UC Berkeley Possibility Lab partnered with HCD to better understand local governments’ processes and challenges related to preparing Housing Element Annual Progress Reports (APR). Because jurisdictions report on their previous year’s housing development progress, our study, which took place in 2025, focused on the APRs for housing moving through the development pipeline in 2024. Broadly, this project was pursued in three sequential phases:

  1. The Possibility Lab research team began data collection in March 2025 with an online survey distributed to all California jurisdictions with an approved 2024 APR, in order to develop a broad understanding of jurisdictions’ various data collection workflows and corresponding challenges.

  2. To establish a more in-depth understanding of specific variations in workflow and ideas for improvement, we then interviewed a subset of survey respondents. This subset was selected based on their jurisdiction’s geographic and demographic characteristics, in order to ensure a diverse sample of interviewees.

  3. Finally, we convened a focus group composed of a further subset of interview participants to facilitate shared learning and glean additional insights from civil servants about their APR data collection processes.

Statewide Survey

The Possibility Lab research team developed a survey instrument that covered four key areas and totaled more than 70 questions. These sections covered:

  1. Information about the Jurisdiction and Survey Respondent

  2. APR Preparation

    1. Staffing, Time, Other Logistics

    2. Data Storage and Compilation

    3. Completing the Form

    4. Data Review and Submission

  3. Respondent Perspectives on APR Processes

  4. Areas and Ideas for Improving APR Processes

The purpose of the survey was to gain a broad understanding of local data collection processes, common definitions or lexicology, technologies used, and other data compilation, storage, review, and submission procedures used to obtain and report APR data to HCD. Importantly, the survey is limited in that it cannot directly measure the accuracy of jurisdictions’ 2024 APRs. The survey included questions related to perceived data accuracy (see Section 2.4); however, because the survey data is self-reported, we cannot draw inferences about objective levels of data accuracy among the jurisdictions represented in our sample. The complete survey instrument is provided in Appendix A.

Survey Recruitment

The survey was administered online and respondents were recruited from the full list of local government staff and/or consultants who had submitted the 2024 APR as of May 31, 2025.

Specifically, once HCD deemed a jurisdiction’s 2024 APR as complete, HCD staff then shared the survey link to the individual who submitted the APR form. The survey was distributed on a rolling basis, as jurisdictions submitted their APRs to HCD between early March and late May 2025. The survey included a screener question that asked if the respondent had worked directly on the 2024 APR to ensure that they were qualified to report on the jurisdiction’s processes.

Survey Respondents

In total, 479 of the 539 jurisdictions32 that were required to submit a complete 2024 APR to HCD (88.9%) had done so at the time of our data collection. Based on our recruitment process, this means that all 479 of these jurisdictions should have received a survey link. Moreover, this means that the survey link was never shared with 60 jurisdictions—more than 10% of the state’s total. As a result, these jurisdictions could not be included in our sample. Because these jurisdictions are already out of compliance with the APR process by choosing not to submit an APR by the April 1 deadline, it is likely that they are not jurisdictions with rigorous APR systems at the local level. Out of the 479 jurisdictions that received a survey link, we received complete survey responses from 173 jurisdictions—a 36.1% response rate of our initial sample and a 32.1% response rate from California’s total jurisdictions that were required to submit a 2024 APR.33

The completed survey sample includes respondents from 146 cities (84.4% of respondents in the sample) and 27 counties (15.6% of respondents in the sample). Individuals from counties, which comprise 10.7% of all California jurisdictions, completed the survey at a higher rate than individuals from cities, and counties are therefore overrepresented in our sample by about 5 percentage points. Jurisdictions with 20,001 to 50,000 residents are also somewhat overrepresented in the sample by about 6 percentage points.

Across California, only 6.1% of jurisdictions—33 total jurisdictions—are officially considered rural counties or cities located in rural counties. Rural jurisdictions are thus overrepresented by about 1.5 percentage points in our sample, which includes 13 survey respondents (7.5%) from jurisdictions that are officially identified by the U.S. Census Bureau as either a rural county or as a city located in a rural county.34

As briefly explained in the previous section, COGs play a large role in how local jurisdictions receive their housing goals through the RHNA process. As such, our survey asked respondents to indicate the COG with which their local government is affiliated.35 The Southern California Association of Governments (SCAG) includes six counties in Southern California and encompasses the greater Los Angeles area, making it the state’s largest COG covering 36.5% of the state’s total jurisdictions. As shown in Table 3, 32.9% of survey respondents reported being affiliated with SCAG, making SCAG jurisdictions just slightly underrepresented in our sample relative to their share of the state by about 3 percentage points. Meanwhile, Bay Area jurisdictions were slightly overrepresented in the sample: 27.7% of respondents reported being affiliated with the Association of Bay Area Governments (ABAG), which includes nine counties and covers 20.4% of all jurisdictions in the state. Most of California’s COGs are represented in the survey sample, though all COGs other than SCAG and ABAG had fewer than 10 survey respondents.

Detailed Study of Selected Jurisdictions

Sampling Criteria

Following the conclusion of the online survey in May 2025, the Possibility Lab research team sought to carry out a more detailed study of 10 jurisdictions in order to better understand their APR data collection processes and further explore potential process documentation and improvements. To select these 10 jurisdictions, we prioritized geographic diversity, specifically seeking to include:

  1. At least one (1) small jurisdiction (60,000 or less in population);

  2. At least one (1) medium-sized jurisdiction (greater than 60,000 population but less than 200,000 population);

  3. At least one (1) large jurisdiction (greater than 200,000 population);

  4. At least three (3) cities;

  5. At least one (1) county;

  6. At least two (2) jurisdictions in Northern California;

  7. At least two (2) jurisdictions in Southern California; and

  8. At least one (1) rural jurisdiction.

In addition to each of these geographic types, we also considered jurisdictions for inclusion in this further data collection effort based on their responses to the online survey, and to ensure we captured a diversity of perspectives and experiences. For this reason, we considered population size, Census-determined levels of urbanity or rurality, whether it is a city or county, and region of the state. Additionally, we considered local governments’ reported staffing levels, whether they hired a consultant or not, use of permitting software, recent changes or upgrades to their processes, APR submission method in 2025, level of recent housing production, and specific topics and problems raised in responses to open-ended survey questions. Within each of these strata, we selected a first-choice jurisdiction and a second-choice jurisdiction that we would recruit if the first choice was unresponsive or declined to participate.

Interviews

We reached out to each jurisdiction selected for this follow-up data collection. Ultimately, we interviewed two local government staff members for about half of the jurisdictions, and interviewed one person for the others, for a total of 17 participants from 11 total jurisdictions. We also interviewed a planner from a land use consulting firm that had worked with three jurisdictions in Northern California on their most recent APRs.

We deliberately designed the sample of interviewees to roughly reflect the characteristics of the survey sample, as well as the range of jurisdictions across the state (see Table 4). In all, eight of the jurisdictions represented by our interview subjects were cities and three were counties, six were located in northern California and five were located in southern California, and two were rural jurisdictions and nine were urban or suburban jurisdictions.

Once the sample was selected, the Possibility Lab team conducted semi-structured interviews between May and July 2025. All interviews were conducted over Zoom and lasted about one hour, on average. These conversations were designed to understand the APR data collection workflow (the collection process for the data that each jurisdiction enters into the Housing Element Annual Progress Report form) in greater detail; to identify similarities and differences in jurisdictions’ data collection workflows and terminology; and to glean insights about how civil servants discuss APR data collection with peers who share their level of expertise.

Focus Group

Following the completion of these interviews, the Possibility Lab research team convened a focus group with two primary aims: (1) to ask additional questions related to how local jurisdictions prepare their APRs, how jurisdictions differ, and how HCD might respond to those differences and support high-quality data collection; and (2) to create an opportunity for local government staff who work on APRs to compare their processes, learn from one another, and develop connections with peers in other jurisdictions.

We invited all of the individuals we had interviewed up to that point to participate in the focus group, which took place in September of 2025. Of the 15 interviewees we invited, eight staff representing six jurisdictions participated in the focus group. Focus group questions centered on process comparisons, potential costs and benefits of a web-based APR form, and jurisdiction capacity and logistics. The focus group was held over Zoom and lasted ninety minutes.

Section 1: APR Form and Requirements

1.1 Components of the 2024 APR Form

State law requires local jurisdictions to submit their APR data annually by April 1 of each year. Specifically, California mandates that all local planning agencies provide an annual report to HCD that gives an update on implementation of their jurisdiction’s housing element and progress toward meeting its housing goals. The APR requires compiling and submitting a wide range of information about various stages of the housing development process (see Appendix Table E1).

Since the law was first adopted in 1965, the relevant statute has been amended many times by the state legislature, including as recently as 2025. In 2017, AB 879 (Chapter 374, Statutes of 2017) required HCD to develop a standard form for each jurisdiction to submit their annual report.38 Since then, legislative amendments often result in changes to the required information that each jurisdiction must report to HCD through the APR process.

HCD publicly shares the “APR Form”—an editable macro-enabled Microsoft Excel workbook—as the mechanism that local jurisdictions must use to submit the APR data to HCD. HCD also provides extensive instructions along with the APR form each year. For the 2024 cycle (which is the specific focus of this study) as well as the most recent 2025 cycle, the instructions cover 33 pages with specific details for each table in the workbook.

When a bill related to the APR becomes law, HCD staff are responsible for modifying the APR submission form (APR form) and updating corresponding instructions to implement the new requirements in the APR form. Depending on the new requirements, some additions are incorporated into existing tables in the form, while other reforms require that a new table be added to the Excel workbook. For example, Table G—which requires data about Locally Owned Lands included in the Housing Element Sites Inventory that have been sold, leased, or otherwise disposed of—was established after AB 1486 (Chapter 664, Statutes of 2019) mandated reporting on the sale or lease of locally owned lands included in the housing element sites inventory.39

Over time, the APR requirements generally have increased and become more labor intensive. Since 2018, more than 90 new data points have been added to the APR form through updated legislation, though many of these fields appear in optional tables. In 2024, the Microsoft Excel APR submission form included 12 different tables where local governments were asked to report various pieces of information. Most of the tables, however, are required only if applicable to the jurisdiction, including Tables E, F, F2, G, H, J, K, and LEAP reporting, and we understand that many jurisdictions do not input information into all of the tables. Nonetheless, the burden of additional reporting requirements competes with other deadlines and planning priorities.

1.2 Reporting Unit-Level Affordability Data in the APR

Throughout this report, we describe findings from focus groups and interviews we conducted with California jurisdictions related specifically to Table A and Table A2 in the APR form. Because these tables require a uniquely granular level of detail compared to other tables, this section elaborates on specific requirements in these tables, as context for later discussion.

The unit of observation in these tables is a single housing project, meaning planners report information on a project-by-project basis in Tables A and A2. This project-level data includes information regarding the expected affordability levels of all units included within every housing project in the jurisdiction’s development pipeline. These tables differ from one another in that Table A collects information on housing projects for which housing development applications have been received by the jurisdiction, whereas Table A2 collects information on housing projects for which applications have been approved, building permits have been issued, and/or construction has been completed.

Table A and Table A2 both include a series of fields, within which specific categories of data are reported in discrete columns. Both Tables A and A2 include a field for the “Project Identifier,” with columns for data categories including “Prior APN,”40 “Current APN,” “Street Address,” “Project Name,” and “Local Jurisdiction Tracking ID.” This identifying information enables longitudinal analysis of a single housing project over time and across APR reporting years, specifically as the project reaches three core development milestones, as previously explained in the Introduction: (1) planning approvals, (2) building approvals, and (3) construction completion. Each of these three milestones can be understood as a ‘triggering event’ that necessitates updated data collection and entry in the APR for the reporting year during which the milestone was reached.

In Table A2, there is a field for each of these milestones, within which columns collect unit-level affordability data. In Table A, there is a similar field for “proposed units,” which likewise includes columns for unit-level affordability data. In all of these fields, planners must report the number of units in a housing project across four affordability brackets: very low-income, low-income, moderate-income, and above moderate-income. With the exception of the above moderate-income bracket, every affordability bracket has two columns: one for deed-restricted units, and another for non-deed-restricted units.

There is quite a lot of complexity when it comes to reporting on housing data, especially when it comes to development activity that spans multiple years. Indeed, the APR instructions make clear that it is highly likely that the same project will be reported in multiple years of APRs. The instructions provide an example that instructs jurisdictions to list a project in three separate APRs if it is entitled in one year, receives the building permit approval the next year, and the construction is completed via the certificate of occupancy in the year following.

At the same time, over the lifecycle of a single housing development (especially a large, multi-family project), the specific number and affordability breakdown of units is liable to change, as emphasized by planners in our study and described throughout this report. The APR, to the best of our understanding, is designed to capture these changes. As such, we can understand each field that is dedicated to a discrete development milestone as capturing ‘point-in-time’ data — that is, unit-level affordability data that is accurate and valid with respect to expected affordability outcomes of the housing project at the time it reached the corresponding development milestone.

For example, imagine a hypothetical housing project with 20 low-income, deed-restricted units that are approved for entitlement in 2023. The jurisdiction would report this project under the ‘approved entitlement’ field of Table A2 in the 2023 APR. Then, let’s say that, in 2024, the project developer secured a new funding source that necessitates an additional 15 low-income units, bringing the total to 35. In 2024, the building permit is also issued for that project. The jurisdiction would thus report this project under the ‘building permit’ field of Table A2 in the 2024 APR, but this time the data would indicate 35 low-income, deed-restricted units. Even though the number of low-income, deed-restricted units for that project is discrepant between the 2023 and 2024 APRs, we would still consider the data accurate and valid, so long as the 2023 APR entitlement field included 20 units and the 2024 APR building permit field included 35 units. Point-in-time data is meant to capture changes along these lines.

When it comes to housing projects with deed-restricted units, it’s also helpful to distinguish ‘development milestones’ from ‘legal milestones.’ In the example above, the building permit approval can be understood as a development milestone that provides an operational authorization to begin construction. In contrast, the updated deed restriction that mandates an additional 15 low-income units can be understood as a legal milestone. While the development milestone serves as the reporting ‘trigger’ for the APR, the legal milestone (i.e., the updated deed restriction) provides the primary source documentation that formalizes the affordability requirements for the newly permitted building. In this example, the legal milestone stems from a financing-related deed restriction. However, legal milestones can also arise from the planning process, such as when affordability commitments are formalized via planning-related deed restrictions to qualify a project for streamlined ministerial approval. As described in Section 3.1.3.c, this distinction between development milestones and legal milestones helps contextualize data collection processes and challenges for reporting deed-restricted units in Table A2.

Section 2: Overview of APR Preparation Process

To better understand how jurisdictions engage in the APR process, we conducted an online survey, a series of semi-structured interviews, and a guided focus group with planners from across California.

Survey data indicate that preparing the Housing Element APR involves a range of tasks, from data collection to final submission. This section describes the overarching workflow of APR preparation observed in our study, as well as where we have identified differences between jurisdictions in their reported processes.

These differences are primarily defined by jurisdiction size. Throughout this section, we thus report survey data findings overall, as well as disaggregated across groups of respondents based on their reported jurisdiction size. For ease of interpretation, we’ve collapsed the jurisdiction size brackets (previously described in Table 2) as follows: (1) fewer than 20,000 residents, (2) 20,000-50,000 residents, (3) 50,001-100,000 residents, and (4) more 100,000 residents.41 We find differences by jurisdiction size regarding the relative share of time dedicated to discrete tasks, the total number of staff involved in the process, and the total amount of time it takes to complete the APR. Generally speaking, we find that the largest jurisdictions spend a relatively greater share of their time cleaning and verifying data, and they also spend more time and require more staff to complete the APR.

2.1 Workflow and Tasks

Table 5 shows the percentage of time survey respondents reported that their jurisdiction spent on each of a set of tasks related to preparing the APR. These tasks include: collecting data (e.g., entering project details into a tracking system and/or gathering untracked project details), inputting data (e.g., transcribing data from tracking systems into the APR form), cleaning data (e.g., removing duplicate entries and ensuring proper formatting), and verifying data (e.g., cross-referencing reported affordability levels with rent listings to ensure accuracy). Additional tasks include coordinating within local government and coordinating with HCD, both of which could potentially occur as part of the aforementioned data tasks.

On average, local governments report spending the largest share of their APR preparation time collecting required data (26.7%), closely followed by time spent inputting data into the APR submission form (25.9%). For some tasks, time allocation varies significantly by jurisdiction size. Compared to the smallest jurisdictions, larger jurisdictions report spending a significantly greater share of their time cleaning and verifying data, and a significantly smaller share of their time collecting and inputting data. The data suggest that large jurisdictions also report spending a significantly greater share of their time coordinating within local government compared to the smallest jurisdictions. We did not identify a significant association between jurisdiction size and share of time spent coordinating with HCD; jurisdictions of all sizes appear to not spend much of their time coordinating with HCD when working on the APR.42

2.2 Staffing and Personnel

Our survey findings suggest that preparing and submitting the Housing Element APR is commonly the responsibility of local planners. Specifically, the survey asked each respondent to write-in both their department and their job title. A majority of survey respondents (53.8%) reported working in the “planning” or “planning and building” department. An even larger majority (75.1%) of survey respondents identified as a planner, with job titles such as Associate Planner or Planning Consultant.

Respondents also reported job titles that reference community development or other local government functions. Specifically, 9.2% of survey respondents (16) reported a title that includes “Community Development,” such as Director of Community Development. About 5% of respondents identified as Housing Program Managers, and another 5% of respondents (9) identified as Management or Financial Analysts in their jurisdictions.

In their survey responses and during our follow-up interviews, individuals described the various ways staffing of the APR process is managed across jurisdictions. For example:

“Typically two planners will work on preparing and gathering data for the APR, however, once the first draft is complete, the Director and Planning Manager will step in to assist with editing and inputting additional information.” (Small city in Southern California)

“The core staff team that primarily manages the APR coordination and submittal process… consists of about 6-10 individuals. However, additional dozens of city staff members from departments citywide are also approached for varying levels of involvement, particularly to provide programmatic updates in Table D.” (Large city in Southern California)

In addition to relying on their internal staff, some local governments also hire external consultants to help them complete the Housing Element APR. In our sample, 13% of survey respondents (22) reported that their jurisdiction had hired a consultant to work on the 2024 APR,44 and these survey respondents represented both very large and very small jurisdictions. For the majority of these cases (81.8%), the respondent identified themselves as the consultant hired by the jurisdiction. Interestingly, two survey respondents who identified as consultants reported that they were hired by multiple jurisdictions to assist with their 2024 APRs, suggesting that some consultants are familiar with multiple jurisdictional contexts.

In our interviews, we heard that a local government’s level of staff capacity was a crucial factor in how difficult or easy it is to complete the APR. In simple terms, having more staff can spread out the workload and reduce the burden on any individual person. Nonetheless, as noted in the previous section, the survey data suggest that many APRs are developed by small teams or even individuals. Roughly half of our survey sample, 96 respondents (55.5%), said that just one or two staff in their local government worked on the 2024 APR.

Table 7 shows reported staffing levels for the APR, categorized by jurisdiction population size. As illustrated in Table 7, larger jurisdictions tend to report having more staff working on their APR.45 About forty percent (40.5%) of jurisdictions with more than 100,000 residents reported that at least 6 staff members had worked on the 2024 APR. However, one of California’s largest cities had just one person who worked on the 2024 APR.

2.2.1 Inter-Departmental Collaboration

According to survey respondents, preparing the Housing Element APR requires significant interdepartmental collaboration. Although preparing and submitting the APR form is commonly managed by planning departments (as previously noted in Section 2.1), many planners reported coordinating with staff from multiple departments as part of their workflow to collect the required APR data. Specifically, 87.3% of survey respondents (151) reported working directly with different departments, divisions, or agencies within their jurisdiction’s local government to collect all the information or data needed to complete the APR. By contrast, just 12.7% of respondents (22) reported no form of interdepartmental collaboration.

Survey respondents indicated that, on average, 2.9 local government departments or agencies contribute to the APR. About three-quarters of survey respondents reported that the building department (77.5%) contributes to their jurisdiction’s APR, and a similar share of respondents (75.1%) reported contributions from their jurisdiction’s planning department.46 With the next most common response, 42.2% said that their local government’s Housing and Community Development department contributes to the APR. See Appendix Table E4.

Participants provided examples of collaboration, including survey respondents who wrote:

“The building and planning divisions work together to pull permits and planning application data. We have a meeting prior to submitting the report to ensure all data is accurate before bringing [the APR] to City Council.” (Large city in Southern California)

“[The] Building Division issues building permits and we coordinate with them to make sure the issued permit information is correct. Our City Manager's office oversees Housing, so we work with them on surplus lands or any housing authority related items, i.e. rent controls on City run projects, etc. and also work with them on Housing Element program implementation tracking.” (Midsize city in Southern California)

2.2.2 Training and Experience

Our survey data suggest that many of the local civil servants who are responsible for preparing and submitting the APR do not have substantial prior experience in doing so. Many survey respondents reported being new to the process this past year (20.8%) or had only been responsible for working on it for 2-3 years (43.9%). About half of respondents (52.9%) said they were not aware or did not expect that they would work on the APR at the time they started in their current position.

We also asked survey respondents if they had previously worked on the Housing Element APR for any other jurisdiction, and 79.2% of respondents (137) reported that they had not. This implies that a large majority of respondents first learned how to complete the Housing Element APR while they were employed by their current local government employer. Taken together, these findings suggest that most APRs are submitted by planners with fewer than 4 years of experience, and their expertise was developed primarily within the unique context of their current jurisdiction.

Though limited in terms of personal experience with the APR, survey respondents commonly reported relying on others who had direct insight into Housing Element program implementation to support their work. Specifically, 73.4% of survey respondents (127) said that someone who had helped prepare their jurisdiction’s current Housing Element also worked on completing Table D of the APR form, the Housing Programs Progress Report, for the 2024 APR.

2.3 Capacity

Preparing the APR takes significant time and effort for local governments, according to planners who participated in our study and independently deduced by the Possibility Lab. In open-ended survey responses, the amount of time it takes to prepare the APR was one of the most commonly described challenges. In interviews, planners emphasized that the APR takes a considerable toll on staff due to the relatively large amount of information required and the short timeline for preparing it. One survey respondent described it to be an overwhelming amount of data to process:

“[The biggest challenge is] the large amount of information that is requested, which takes a lot of staff time. We are trying to mitigate that by updating our software and systems to better capture this information, but this also takes staff resources. We anticipate that HCD will continue to ask for more/new/different data in the future, which will continue to take more staff resources to find that data and continually update our systems/ software to capture it.” (Midsize city in Central Coast)

Preparing the APR also affects jurisdictions’ financial resources. State law requires local governments to complete an APR form that can require dozens of hours but does not provide consistent funding to cover the associated costs of staff time nor expenses related to software systems or hiring consultants. Section 3.1.2.a includes further discussion of the costs of permit tracking software.

Figure 7 presents survey responses regarding the time of year when jurisdictions started preparing the 2024 APR. According to respondents, most jurisdictions started working on the 2024 APR in January or February of 2025, though over a quarter of jurisdictions reportedly started in or before December 2024. Likewise, many of the planners we interviewed told us that the APR is one of their primary responsibilities for several weeks at the beginning of each year.

Staff most commonly reported spending 3 to 5 hours per week working on the APR, and the median amount of time per week is 6 to 10 hours. As presented in Table 8, larger jurisdictions reported spending more hours per week working on the APR.47
