Based on the number of hours spent working on the APR per week and month in which the jurisdiction started working on the APR, we calculated a rough estimate of the total number of hours each jurisdiction spent preparing the 2024 APR.48 Below we present estimates of the median total hours that jurisdictions of different sizes devoted to the 2024 APR. These estimates are not definitive, as they were developed through a “back-of-the-envelope” calculation and are based on survey respondents’ own, unverified estimates. But we believe these figures, especially the medians, are useful for giving a general sense of how many hours jurisdictions spend on the APR. As expected (because they have more project-level data to locate, clean, and verify), the largest jurisdictions report spending more hours on the APR than the smallest jurisdictions, as illustrated in Figure 8.49

Time spent preparing the APR also reportedly prevents or delays staff from doing other parts of their jobs. As presented in Figure 9 (and Appendix Table E2), among the 155 jurisdictions that did not hire a consultant to work on the APR, a majority of survey respondents (74.8%) reported that they put other work on hold while they work on the APR. Furthermore, as shown in Figure 10 (and Appendix Table E2), staff in some of these jurisdictions reportedly work overtime to complete the APR, as indicated by the 55 respondents (35.5%) who said that their team worked extra hours to finish the 2024 APR on time (such as by working on weekends or through lunch breaks).

This suggests there may be a significant substitution effect of APR processes; the hours planners spend working on the APR is time that is not spent reviewing project applications and shepherding projects through the planning approvals process or, in the case of long-range planners, working on ordinances to implement state housing laws. As described by three survey respondents:

“We have two long-range planners. One staff planner takes on the task of completing the APR, which takes many hours of staff time, leaving only one planner to complete long-range planning projects (such as implementing our housing element objectives) during the time it takes to complete the APR.” (Midsize city in Central Coast)

“I, as the Planning Manager, dedicate my own time toward preparing the city's Housing Element APR, because I do not have the staff capacity to pull my team away from their other work.” (Small city in Central Coast)

"While we have sufficient staff, APR work always requires shifting of project time and resources, and in some cases, may delay other project work." (Large county in the Bay Area)

We asked local government staff in jurisdictions that did not hire a consultant to develop their APR whether their level of staffing was adequate to complete the APR, and responses from this group of 155 jurisdictions were split. Half (49.7%)% of survey respondents (77) reported that they would benefit from additional staff capacity. By contrast, 45.8% of survey respondents (71) reported that they have sufficient staff capacity. Notably, only two respondents (1.3%) reported that they have more than enough staff capacity. Staff perceptions of their jurisdiction’s level of staff capacity do not vary significantly by population size or region (as determined by COG). However, they are significantly associated with having reported working extra hours and putting other work on hold, as well as average hours per week spent working on the APR and the month the jurisdiction began working on the APR.50

2.4 Perceptions of the APR Process and Form

Some of the local government staff we interviewed expressed uncertainty about the accuracy of information reported in their APR submissions, and multiple planners noted that mistakes in their reported data are sometimes identified after submission.51 Among the planners we interviewed, planners from smaller jurisdictions more commonly expressed confidence in the accuracy of their reported data because it had been reviewed thoroughly in advance of submission. In contrast, the volume of data that larger jurisdictions report was cited by interviewees from those jurisdictions as a likely source of error that is difficult to catch in advance of submission due to time and/or capacity constraints. As one planner described:

“As a large jurisdiction, collecting and ensuring all the data is accurate is challenging. This is not only due to the volume of permits we process but also due to the amount of information about each permit HCD requested.” (Large city in Bay Area)

As we discuss later in Section 3.1.3, local government staff may not have these concerns across all of the data throughout the APR, but specifically about certain data points they provide. For example, affordability information about individual units typically becomes more reliable relative to actual housing outcomes as the project advances through the development pipeline. In the focus group, a few planners agreed that, by the time the project receives building permit approvals, the makeup of units by affordability level will likely not change. The quote below highlights that some planners are seemingly uncertain about what constitutes accurate reporting of application data, given that stated affordability levels at early development stages may not correspond with actual housing outcomes.

“If the state really wants to know exactly the level of affordability and number of units at each level, then what we are submitting as a planning agency is not 100% accurate. And that’s because I have no idea if any of these projects, down the road, will get some grant or tax credit or loan, and those might have terms and conditions beyond and above what we [the jurisdiction] require under the inclusionary [zoning] ordinance or density bonus ordinance.” (Large jurisdiction in Southern California)

Despite reported concerns, all of the planners we interviewed expressed their commitment to providing accurate data that is useful to the state. Staff from a few jurisdictions explicitly told us that they always want to “play by the rules,” do the best they can, and comply with state laws. When asked how they would respond if HCD rejected their APR submission and asked them to submit a significantly revised version, planners from multiple jurisdictions said it would be a high priority for their department to provide a revised APR promptly.

In addition to the interviews, our survey asked respondents how much they agree or disagree that the APR process and form structure enable them to report complete and accurate housing information for their jurisdiction. As illustrated in Figure 11 below (and Appendix Table E3), respondents from jurisdictions with populations between 20,000 and 50,000 reported the highest levels of agreement, while the smallest jurisdictions reported the most disagreement.52 Analyzing the sample as a whole, we find that a majority of survey respondents (72.3%) said they agree with this statement, though just 16.8% of respondents (29) said they strongly agree, and the other 55.5% of respondents (96) said that they somewhat agree. Only 6.9% of respondents (12) said they somewhat disagree that the APR process and form enable them to submit accurate data, and no respondents in our sample said they strongly disagree. These data indicate that a majority of respondents lean positively about the ability of the APR process and form to result in complete and accurate data. However, because just 16.8% of jurisdictions strongly agreed, it stands to reason that the remainder may have, to varying degrees, some concerns about the APR process and/or form.

*The survey question reads, “To what extent do you agree or disagree that the APR process and form structure enables you to report complete and accurate housing information?”

Acknowledging the variation among survey participants in their views on how the APR process and form enables complete and accurate reporting, it’s important to underscore that our survey does not directly measure the empirical accuracy of jurisdictions’ APR data submissions. In conversations with our team, HCD staff expressed confidence that the APR dataset is largely accurate in measuring overall housing development activity as well as trends, particularly at the statewide and regional levels.

The overall accuracy of the APR data can be contextualized through comparisons to other datasets. For example, the annual US Census Building Permit Survey (BPS) provides a comparable housing dataset in which “permit-issuing places” across the United States (including the California jurisdictions in our study) voluntarily report the number of units in every structure for which they’ve issued a permit.53 Whereas the APR form collects the number of units on a project-by-project basis, the BPS form collects the total number of buildings and units by structure type, aggregated within four discrete reporting brackets for (1) single-family houses, (2) two-unit buildings, (3) three- and four-unit buildings, and (4) five-or-more unit buildings.

In Table 9 below, we present the total number of permitted units in California between 2019 and 2025, as reported in the APR and BPS datasets, respectively. In Figure 12, we compare overall trends in the APR and BPS datasets by plotting the annual percent change in the number of permitted units.54

When comparing the two datasets, we find similar overall trends in the number of permitted units, where the direction of change is consistent in each dataset. For example, both datasets demonstrate a decrease in the number of permitted units between 2019 and 2020, followed by an increase between 2020 and 2021. While similar in their directional trends, the datasets differ in that, each year, the APR dataset includes roughly 6–20% more units permitted than the BPS dataset.

This pattern could be attributable to differences in underlying inclusion criteria. When completing the BPS form, respondents are instructed to exclude particular types of ADUs and all mobile homes, whereas the APR includes all ADUs and all mobile homes.55 Because the APR does not differentiate between types of ADUs that overlap with the ADU distinctions applied in the BPS, and because the BPS does not disaggregate ADUs within its reporting categories at all, we are unable to definitively discern whether the difference between the datasets’ counts of total permitted units is attributable to the BPS’s more limited inclusion criteria. When excluding ADUs and mobile homes from the APR, the total number of permitted units in the BPS exceeds that of the APR. These patterns are explored in Figure 13, where we compare the unit counts between the BPS overall and the APR with and without ADUs and mobile homes.

In addition to differences in inclusion criteria, the APR and BPS differ in that compliance with the APR is required for California jurisdictions, whereas the BPS is voluntary. Perhaps unsurprisingly, then, the Census BPS reported a lower national response rate of 81% in 2024,56 whereas we calculate the APR’s response rate as 95% for the same year.57 Given its voluntary basis and lower response rate, the BPS uses imputation techniques to mitigate resultant sample limitations, which could conceivably contribute to different overall permitted unit counts in the BPS compared to the APR.58

Notably, the imputation approach introduces statistical uncertainty around the BPS estimates. After imputation, the BPS provides an estimate for 100% of jurisdictions. Because the imputation procedures are based on the prior year’s estimate for a place, there may be less year-to-year change in the BPS data. Moreover, because the BPS provides an estimated count for 100% of jurisdictions, and the APR count only covers 95% of jurisdictions, it’s not surprising that the BPS’s total estimate is higher after removing ADUs and mobile homes from the APR count.

Taken as a whole, the findings from our study reinforce the importance of investigating and improving upon the APR process and form to lower the burden of reporting accurate data, so that the APR dataset can continue contributing to evidence-policymaking in California.

Section 3: Data Collection for the APR

As previously emphasized in Section 2.2.1, our survey findings suggest that data collection for the APR involves substantial interdepartmental collaboration. In response to an open-ended question about the biggest challenges in preparing the APR, 36 survey respondents (20.8%) described challenges about gathering data. Among those respondents, 8 respondents specifically mentioned the challenge of gathering data for the APR form from other departments or divisions.

Housing development data is collected synchronously and retrospectively among the jurisdictions included in our study.59

  • Synchronous data collection occurs in real time: planners and local government staff log housing data from primary source materials — such as applications, entitlement records, building permits, and certificates of occupancy — as they are first processed.

  • Retrospective data collection occurs after time has passed: planners are tracking down information that was not systematically collected and/or recorded in jurisdictions’ standard documentation throughout the reporting year, usually through follow-up communications between departments and developers.

As described in Section 3.1.1, our findings suggest that jurisdictions vary in the extent to which they collect, consolidate, and link project-level data across development milestones on a regular basis throughout the reporting year. For example, in the building permit approval process, if a jurisdiction’s application materials do not ask developers for the specific rents or affordability levels of units included in the project (see Section 3.1.3), then related APR data points may not be systematically collected as a matter of course. In these instances, retrospective data collection serves as a secondary measure for planners to capture missing data points when preparing the APR form.

As elaborated upon in Section 3.2.2, data points related to housing development that commonly require retrospective data collection include the project’s affordability level, financing information, tenure, and use of streamlining laws or incentives (e.g., density bonuses). Moreover, as described in Section 3.2, information related to the implementation of housing element programs (required in Table D) is often collected and consolidated retrospectively.

3.1 Collecting Housing Development Data

The findings from our survey, interviews, and focus group suggest that planners sometimes struggle to accurately link project data across the different phases of the development pipeline, even within their internal data tracking processes. As elaborated below in Section 3.1.3, the challenge may stem, at least in part, from governance structures, under which planning approvals, building permit approvals, and construction completion records are potentially managed by different departments within a local government.

Moreover, by our own observation (see Section 3.1.3.b), there is no standardized template or form through which departments collect information from developers across the development stages. Instead, each department within each local government seemingly designs their own forms that developers fill out to provide project information and secure the necessary approvals. In some cases, jurisdictions may not consistently assign a unique identifier to a given project as it progresses through the development phases, which can obscure linkages between project data across different documentation sources. The findings suggest that the underlying documentation processes are a potential root cause of the difficulties faced when collecting and reporting APR data, particularly for Tables A and A2.

In an ideal arrangement, a planner preparing the APR would have all the information they need for the APR already consolidated, so that preparing the APR each year is primarily a matter of inputting already consolidated data into the APR form. Our survey findings suggest this scenario is not the norm. Only half of survey respondents (51.4%) reported that the information required to complete the APR (particularly information on project applications, planning approvals, and building permit approvals for Tables A and A2) was mostly consolidated, while the remainder said information was mostly in different places.

Figure 14 (and Appendix Table E4) shows the breakdown of survey responses to this question by jurisdiction size. Compared to smaller jurisdictions, larger jurisdictions were significantly more likely to report that their data is mostly consolidated.60 The reverse is also true. As displayed in Figure 14, the smallest jurisdictions were nearly twice as likely as the largest jurisdictions to report that their data was not consolidated (60% compared to 32.4%). One survey respondent from a small city described how they manage their lack of data consolidation as follows:

“Our jurisdiction does not have a centralized database or permitting system where we can store and output the necessary data for the APR. I maintain about four different spreadsheets that track various information from the planning and building divisions that contribute toward the APR data requirements….” (Small city in Central Coast)

Data consolidation is a potentially important contributor to feasibly reporting complete and accurate APR data. Respondents who reported that their jurisdiction’s information is mostly consolidated in one system were significantly more likely to agree that the APR process and form structure enables them to report complete and accurate housing information for their jurisdiction.61 These results reflect subjective perceptions of data accuracy and are thus limited in terms of providing insights about the determinants of objective data accuracy outcomes. Nonetheless, these findings underscore the potential value of effective data consolidation among local jurisdictions, either through synchronous data collection practices or more periodic retrospective data collection practices throughout the reporting year. In Section 3.1.1 below, we elaborate on the kinds of data sources that jurisdictions rely upon to collect APR data, the varied range of which is consistent with the relatively widespread lack of data consolidation among jurisdictions included in our survey.

3.1.1 Data Sources for Housing Development Data

Here, we present survey findings on the kinds of data sources that jurisdictions rely upon to collect APR data, the varied range of which is consistent with the relatively widespread lack of data consolidation observed in our study.

As presented in Table 10, 147 survey respondents (85.0%) reported that they obtain housing development data for the APR in their team’s own digital files or data storage systems, and nearly all of the remaining respondents reported that they use digital resources from other teams or departments in their local government. In total, 167 respondents (96.5%) indicated use of digital sources from their local government for APR data. While 38 survey respondents (22.0%) make use of paper documents, each of these respondents also reported using digital sources, suggesting exclusive reliance on paper documentation for APR data is minimal.

A majority of survey respondents (61.3%) reported that conversations with planning and/or building department staff are a source of APR data; however, this reliance is typically in addition to other sources. Just two jurisdictions reportedly rely on solely conversations with planning and/or building department staff.62

3.1.2 Systems for Synchronous Housing Development Data Collection

As part of the housing development process, jurisdictions receive applications and process planning and building approvals throughout the reporting year. Our findings suggest that permit tracking software—also referred to as government technology (“gov tech”) software—is a primary mechanism for synchronous data collection, through which jurisdictions continuously collect information from primary source documentation and log it in a data storage system. Ideally, these systems would enable jurisdictions to translate routine administrative documentation into trackable data.

Among jurisdictions that completed the survey, 151 respondents (87.3%) reported that their jurisdiction uses some kind of gov tech software to track housing projects across development milestones and collect data from applications, planning approvals, building permit approvals, and construction completion. Moreover, all of the local government staff we interviewed reported that their jurisdiction uses some kind of gov tech software to track projects. Notably, even among the survey respondents who reported using Microsoft Excel for tracking, the majority (18 out of 25) also reported using a gov tech software system. These findings suggest that such systems are crucial to a local government’s day-to-day operations, and, if programmed well, can serve as a centralized repository of housing data that planners consult when preparing the APR.

3.1.2.a Permit Tracking Software Used for Synchronous Data Collection

According to survey respondents, jurisdictions rely on a range of specific permit tracking software services. As presented in Table 11, Accela and TRAKiT from Central Square Technologies are the most common permit tracking software among the jurisdictions that completed our survey, with 33 and 36 out of 173 jurisdictions using these, respectively. Another 32 of these jurisdictions use software from Tyler Technologies, including Enterprise Planning and Licensing (EP&L), EnerGov, and EDEN. We identified 11 jurisdictions that reported using multiple gov tech software systems to track permits.

Table 12 below presents our findings regarding the different kinds of gov tech software that survey respondents reported using across jurisdictions of different sizes. Among survey respondents from the largest jurisdictions (with populations exceeding 100,000 residents), Accela was the most commonly reported software (45.9%), followed by TRAKiT (18.9%) and Tyler Technologies (13.5%). Small jurisdictions with 20,000-50,000 residents and mid-sized jurisdictions with 50,001-100,000 residents also reported using Accela (14.0% and 19.4%, respectively); however, these jurisdictions more commonly use TRAKiT or Tyler Technologies, with about 20-30% of jurisdictions in these size brackets reporting these software platforms. Meanwhile, the smallest jurisdictions (with populations under 20,000 residents) very minimally report using Accela (5.5%) and instead reporting relying on a wide range of software options, including TRAKiT (14.5%) and Tyler Technologies (10.9%) as well as OpenGov (7.3%), iWorQ (10.9%), and other software (25.5%).

These patterns in software used across jurisdictions of varying sizes may reflect software systems’ costs and jurisdictions’ ability to afford them. The prices of permit tracking software vary based on several factors, including the number of employees accessing the system, the sophistication of data tracking, and integration with other local data systems. Implementation can also impose significant additional costs, depending on the degrees of customization and training. Local jurisdictions can spend anywhere from $10,000 to more than $1,000,000 per year on permit tracking software licensing and upgrades. Some companies target larger jurisdictions by offering more features at a higher price, while others serve smaller jurisdictions at a more affordable price.63

3.1.3 Challenges in Housing Development Data Collection

3.1.3.a Inter-Departmental Collaboration and Related Software Constraints

Permit software is typically shared across multiple departments within a local government. When asked which departments use the permit software, survey respondents selected, on average, 3.6 different departments or agencies. Table 13 shows the departments or divisions within local government that can access a shared permit tracking software, according to survey respondents. Many jurisdictions reported that it can be a challenge to ensure that all local staff are inputting data into the permit tracking system accurately and completely. Specifically, interviewees from three jurisdictions mentioned that the various local government staff who input data into their data storage systems do so in different ways, often emphasizing that there are differences between how planning and building department staff manage data. A planner from one large city indicated a desire for better training of local staff who do data entry because they sometimes identify inaccuracies in the information entered into their jurisdiction’s permit tracking system.

Interviewees from some of California's largest jurisdictions reported that there are dozens or hundreds of planners reviewing projects and entering information into their data systems, plus similar numbers of permit technicians in the building department. According to these interviewees, this extensive interdepartmental collaboration can introduce errors and inconsistencies into data points that are later utilized as the basis for APR reporting, compounding any natural tendency for human error in high-volume data entry.

A key topic during the interviews and focus group was how the effectiveness of permit tracking software systems can be limited by how they are configured. Study participants described that it can be difficult to tailor software systems to specific APR requirements because different departments within the same local government often use a shared software platform. In separate interviews, four staff reported that they cannot unilaterally customize how data is stored or produced because it is collected by other departments. One staff member emphasized that, because departments across their jurisdiction use the same software, it takes significant bureaucratic buy-in to make any changes to better reflect the APR. Two staff also reported that their own department's software is not customized for the APR because they do not have the capacity to update it. In the focus group, one planner explained that their jurisdiction cannot customize their software exclusively for the APR because they must report the same housing production data for other purposes, such as the California Department of Finance’s annual Housing Unit Survey. This feedback suggests that there are significant capacity and coordination barriers to effectively customizing software to meet the data requirements of the APR.

3.1.3.b Inconsistent Documentation of Unique Project Identifiers

A recurring theme described in our study was linking project-level data across development milestones. Specifically, three interviewees from large jurisdictions described difficulty linking a development across planning approvals and building permit approvals. This challenge is especially pertinent to Tables A and A2. In both tables (as previously described in Section 1.2), planners provide information for the “Project Identifier” field. In each table, this field includes five columns, which are described in Table 14 below.

Some columns in the Project Identifier field are required (i.e., Current Assessor’s Parcel Number (APN) and Street Address) and some are optional (i.e., Prior APN, Project Name, and Local Jurisdiction Tracking ID). When reporting project-level data at different development milestones, planners are expected to ensure projects are accurately linked in their APRs. In straightforward housing projects, project-level data across development milestones can be reliably linked using the Current APN. However, if a project’s APN changes throughout the development process, or if there is a subdivision that results in multiple new APNs for the same project, the jurisdiction is expected to link the project-level data by providing a Prior APN or a Local Jurisdiction Tracking ID.

To ensure accurate linkages across development milestones when preparing the APR, jurisdictions would ideally have well-designed systems for ensuring that all building permit approvals and construction completion records are easily traceable to corresponding planning approvals and deed restriction documentation. Our findings suggest this is not always the case. Moreover, there’s some indication that providing accurate APNs is less straightforward than might otherwise be assumed.

In at least a few large jurisdictions we spoke with, the planning and building departments maintain separate systems for logging project data, and staff are not confident in their ability to accurately link planning approval records and building permit approval records when preparing the APR. Some jurisdictions link entries using APNs, though they acknowledge that this has limitations given that APNs can change when parcels are divided or merged. Other jurisdictions report not having APNs for projects at the time of entitlement or when building permits are issued. One planner described this challenge as follows:

“[The biggest challenge is] the requirement to include an APN with the housing data. In [our] County, typically the APN is not available at the time of building permit issuance, and therefore the APN is not in the City's systems. Finding the APN from County maps takes a long time.” (Midsize city in Southern California)

Interviewees described other linking challenges related to their software tracking systems, emphasizing that their software is not always well-suited for large developments with multi-generational planning approvals and building permit approvals. An individual project that goes through the approval and permitting process in a relatively linear way is potentially easiest to track in the software, particularly if the project has one APN that does not change throughout its development. Conversely, it can be more challenging for large, master development-type projects that begin with a single, tentative tract map planning approval that ultimately yields multiple buildings developed over time, each with their own building permit. Subdividing a large piece of land into multiple parcels results in the creation of new APNs and addresses. Cities and counties that have these types of “family tree projects” described particular challenges managing all of the related records.

These kinds of large developments are liable to reach different development milestones in different APR reporting years. As a result, planners are expected to report a project of this kind in multiple APRs. The APR instruction document clarifies the requirements for reporting in these scenarios, as presented in Table 15 below.

Table 15. Quoted instructions from HCD regarding how to report developments spanning multiple years

“Development activity spanning multiple years: It is highly likely that the same project will be reported in multiple years of APRs. For example, a project should be listed in three separate APRs if it is entitled in one year, receives the building permit the next year, and the certificate of occupancy in the year following.”

“In scenarios where development activity spans multiple years, the jurisdiction must only report activity that occurred within the reporting year. For example, if a project received building permits in 2025, but received entitlements in 2024, the 2025 APR must only include the building permit information (fields 7, 8, and 9). Activity from prior years may be included but it is not required.”

Hypothetically, the data entry burden on planners is reduced by the lack of requirements to include prior activity in the APRs for every reporting year in which a development milestone is reached. However, in practice, planners must be able to link data across these different milestones, if not for their own documentation purposes, then at least for the sake of providing accurate Project Identifier information in Tables A and A2. When these development milestones are overseen by different departments within local government, the demands on interdepartmental coordination are increased and so too are the challenges of ensuring accurate reporting of APR data. An interviewee from a large jurisdiction described the challenge as follows:

"Ever since the law was changed... that we need to connect the [planning approval] to the building permit side, that makes it so much harder. Because in the county, [the building department] is part of public works. In order to make sure that our two datasets are connected, you have to try to remove a lot of files between two different departments.... The preparation of the APR requires a lot of manual work, like ‘How do I connect this building permit to the planning entitlement that was approved like two years ago?’ And if it's a bigger project, like a master development, subdivision... it's even harder. It's not like a simple, one-site plan approval for one house or an ADU, where you can find a one-to-one connection.... Eventually [you have to do] matching of the building permit of one individual home or individual condo unit back to that big [planning approval]." (Large jurisdiction in Southern California)

This interviewee described how challenges linking project-level data can sometimes be attributed to a systematic cause—for example, the building department assigns a project a different identifier than what the planning department uses. One of the potential benefits of technology solutions is to be able to link all of the records for the same project, but gov tech solutions are only as good as their underlying documentation sources. By our own observation, the local application materials used by jurisdictions in their development processes do not consistently assign each project a unique project identifier that is recorded across each development milestone. Hypothetically, this kind of unique project identifier could be reported in the APR as the “Local Jurisdiction Tracking ID,” thus resolving the shortcomings of APNs for linking project-level data across milestones.

To make this assessment, we analyzed as many building permit application materials as were publicly available for the jurisdictions included in our interview sample. Our assumption is that, if jurisdictions assign a unique project identifier as part of their documentation flow and synchronous data collection practices, then we would expect to see a field on building permit applications where developers are asked to provide the unique project identifier assigned to their project at the entitlement stage.

Out of the 10 jurisdictions in our interview sample for which a building permit application form was publicly available, only two jurisdictions have applications where a unique identifier or a permit number for the project is collected. One application form used in a large jurisdiction includes a field asking: “Is this application related to any other permit or complaint (yes/no)?” and “If yes, indicate permit #, planning case file #, or complaint #.” Another application form used in a small jurisdiction includes a field asking for the “Permit #,” but it is unclear whether the developer provides this information or if it is later filled in by a civil servant upon approving the permit.

With the exception of the materials from these two jurisdictions, all other building permit applications do not ask for a project identifier and instead simply collect an address or APN. For reasons described above, an address or APN is not a very reliable basis for linking projects, because addresses and APNs are not always generated at early stages and may change over the course of a multi-generational development. Notably, the building permit application form for the jurisdiction quoted above only collects an address.

Given the project linking complexities described by study participants, and in light of our own analysis of local application materials, we suspect that the inconsistent documentation of unique project identifiers in jurisdictions’ documentation flow and synchronous data collection practices is a primary reason jurisdictions might struggle to prepare the APR completely and accurately.

3.1.3.c Difficulty Tracking Affordability Data Across Development and Legal Milestones

Gathering data on housing unit affordability was described as a particular challenge by study participants from many jurisdictions. A majority of survey respondents (60%) indicated that their permit tracking system does not track unit affordability data for all types of permits. This creates a disconnect with the APR requirements. As described in Section 1.2, Tables A and A2 require jurisdictions to report the number of deed- and non-deed-restricted units by affordability bracket. If a jurisdiction reports deed-restricted units for a given project, they must also report relevant project-level information regarding streamlining provisions, density bonuses, financial assistance programs, and the type of deed restriction that formalizes any affordability requirements associated with these benefits.

In open-ended survey responses, 36 survey respondents described in further detail how their jurisdiction’s software doesn’t track all of the information required by the APR. The most common types of information described as not being tracked were unit affordability levels, financing information, tenure, and use of streamlining laws or density bonuses. When this is the case, respondents reported having to pull certain data points one-by-one, sometimes hundreds of times over, when preparing the 2024 APR. According to interviewees, this retrospective data collection can be a time-consuming process for many planners working on the APR.

One interviewee from a medium-sized jurisdiction that uses EnerGov described how their jurisdiction does not track affordability levels in their software and, therefore, relies on a senior planner’s excel spreadsheet when preparing affordability data for the APR. According to the interviewee, the jurisdiction’s staff is aging and has been resistant to technological changes that might have enabled software improvements for synchronous data collection.

The survey specifically asked respondents how their jurisdiction determines which projects are eligible for streamlining under state law, such as SB 423 (Chapter 778, Statutes of 2023)64 or AB 2011 (Chapter 647, Statutes of 2022),65 and how their jurisdiction tracks this information. By far the most common response, 110 respondents (63.6%) reported that their jurisdiction figures out which projects are eligible for streamlining when they are working on the APR. Of these, 66 respondents only selected “We figure it out when completing the APR” and do not have another method of tracking this information, suggesting to us that retrospective data collection for Table A2 at the time of APR form preparation is potentially widespread.

Furthermore, according to study participants, developers are often not certain what their funding sources are going to be when they submit an application, as they may still be trying to secure sufficient financial assistance. In fact, securing financing can sometimes follow planning approvals. The California Tax Credit Allocation Committee, which awards Low Income Housing Tax Credits (LIHTC), requires applicants to provide evidence that they have received local land use approvals, incentivizing developers to seek these approvals through entitlement before confirming the project’s funding or details of its affordability.66 Consequently, the reported affordability levels at the application and planning approval stages may change, because the developer secures funding sources with new affordability requirements.

By our own observation and reasoning, the absence of robust synchronous data collection practices for project-level affordability data on deed-restricted units may be related to the discrepancy between development milestones and legal milestones, as previously described in Section 1.2. For projects with deed-restricted units, the APR is asking jurisdictions to provide unit-level affordability data that is formalized through legal milestones (e.g., covenants and regulatory agreements made pursuant to planning- and financing-related deed restrictions, where developers commit to a set number of affordable units in the project). However, the development milestones around which Table A2 is organized (i.e., planning approvals, building permits, and construction completion records) are not necessarily the legal mechanism through which a developer’s affordability commitments are formalized.

As a result, the APR is essentially asking jurisdictions to report "point-in-time data" related to development milestones, but the project-level affordability data derives from legal mechanisms that do not necessarily occur at the same administrative junctures or even within the same department that oversees the development milestone. For example, if seeking LIHTC funding, a project could plausibly formalize financing-related commitments to deed-restricted units after receiving planning approvals and before receiving a building permit, thus divorcing the legal milestone from the development milestones altogether. Consider another example where the building department is separate from the planning department that formalizes deed-restrictions related to ministerially-streamlined entitlements. When the building department issues permit approvals, their documentation may not collect the specific unit-level affordability data formalized at the planning approval stage.

Unless a jurisdiction’s documentation flow and software system are set up to (1) assign a unique project identifier to each project and (2) collect point-in-time, project-level affordability data at the application, planning approval, building permit approval, and construction completion stages, then the APR requirements would seemingly necessitate interdepartmental collaboration on a project-by-project basis when preparing the APR, in order to link that project’s development milestones to its underlying legal milestones.

This interdepartmental collaboration could take various forms, reflecting the variation across jurisdictions in the specific governance structures under which development milestones and legal milestones are administered. In an interview with one large jurisdiction, a planner described how their team consults underlying covenant documentation to report affordability levels for projects at the stage of construction completion. In contrast, two planners from small jurisdictions said they reach out to developers directly to seek affordability information when preparing the APR. These examples reflect the kinds of retrospective data collection practices that planners resort to when completing the APR, in the absence of synchronous data collection practices that might otherwise bridge the gap between legal and development milestones in order to consistently track a project’s deed-restricted affordability levels.

To gain further insight into jurisdictions’ documentation flow, we analyzed the publicly accessible application materials of jurisdictions included in our interview sample. Our assumption is that, if jurisdictions have synchronous data collection practices for tracking affordability data across legal and development milestones, then we would expect to see a field on building permit applications where developers are asked to provide the expected affordability breakdown of units and any associated streamlining, density bonus, or financial assistance provisions. We were able to access an online building permit application for 10 out of the 11 jurisdictions in our interview sample. For all 10 jurisdictions, we found no indication that this kind of information regarding project-level affordability is collected at the building permit stage, thus reflecting a potential structural gap in jurisdictions’ documentation flow where the development milestone is decoupled from the project’s affordability data. These gaps in the documentation chain may increase the need for onerous retrospective data collection when planners are preparing the APR.

3.1.3.d Difficulty Collecting Affordability Data for Non-Deed-Restricted Units

In the absence of comprehensive synchronous data collection practices, collecting affordability data when preparing the APR can be challenging, regardless of whether the project includes deed-restricted or non-deed-restricted units. However, when it comes to non-deed-restricted units, planners may struggle with a unique set of challenges. Whereas the affordability of deed-restricted units is a contracted agreement, underpinned by legal milestones, the affordability of non-deed-restricted units is a market condition, which requires estimation on the part of jurisdictions when preparing the APR.

In some small or midsized jurisdictions, most or all of the non-deed-restricted affordable units are ADUs. In addition to surveys and online research to estimate affordability, some jurisdictions rely on existing formulas. Several Bay Area jurisdictions wrote in the survey that they use ABAG’s guidance on estimating ADU affordability levels, and at least one jurisdiction wrote that they made use of SCAG’s ADU affordability estimates. One planner described how their jurisdiction estimates the affordability level of ADUs as follows:

“[We conducted] phone surveys to those who constructed ADUs in the reporting year. [We use] market rate analysis to determine a dollar/square foot and the affordability calculator. SFRs [single-family rentals] were studied using published sales prices and the valuation of permits.” (Midsize city in Northern California)

Throughout the development pipeline, planning departments are not always aware of the price at which completed units are being rented or sold. HCD requires jurisdictions to report units without a deed restriction as above moderate-income, unless the jurisdiction provides an affordability justification described in the instructions. In some parts of the state, however, there are non-deed-restricted units that may in reality sell or rent at a price that is affordable to moderate- or lower-income households, and the local government staff must use research or inference to figure out how much non-deed restricted units cost to rent. One planner described the burden on local jurisdictions that comes with reporting non-deed-restricted affordability data:

“HCD staff has not done the work to educate jurisdictions on best practices to collect a dwelling unit's affordability. Planning Staff has had to use their best judgment and own research to report on a building permit's affordability. For instance, land value + improvement value does not equate to the sale price of the property. Planning staff has to use additional research per building permit to figure out if a dwelling unit will be affordable.“ (Midsize city in the Sacramento area)

Seven survey respondents wrote comments indicating that their jurisdictions make use of the HCD affordability calculator, which estimates the lowest affordability level of a housing unit based on its characteristics and some built-in assumptions. The affordability calculator requires inputting the unit’s rent or sales price. Jurisdictions gather this information using the previously described methods or use estimates based on typical rents or sales prices in the area. Other jurisdictions simply input the project valuation.

Column AN67 in Table A2 of the APR form asks for justification for why non-deed restricted units are affordable to moderate- or lower-income households. Survey respondents reported a range of additional sources for completing this column. Most survey respondents (61.3%) obtain this information from their or their colleagues' knowledge of specific projects. Others rely on their permit tracking system or data storage systems for information on why or how units are affordable (20.8%). Jurisdictions ranged significantly in terms of the resources they put towards completing Column AN of Table A2, with some conducting multiple steps of research and consulting outside resources and others operating off of one or two blanket assumptions.

3.2 Collecting Data on Housing Element and RHNA Progress

3.2.1 Data Sources for Housing Element Programs and RHNA Goals

Reporting program implementation status updates in Table D is the component of the APR where respondents reported the most inter-departmental coordination, as it requires gathering information from several different local government departments. Indeed, as shown in Table 18, about 75% of survey respondents indicated that they send emails to or have conversations with staff who know about the progress made on Housing Element programs in order to gather the information necessary for Table D.

In many cases, the person leading the APR described having to do a significant amount of coordination. This can include figuring out the right contact person for each program, reaching out to them, explaining what the APR is and what they need, following up with reminders, and more. Some large jurisdictions have over 100 Housing Element programs, which are implemented by a dozen or more departments, divisions, and agencies (and sometimes multiple staff members in each), creating a scenario where compiling data for Table D can require the collaboration of dozens of people.

3.2.2 Using the APR Form to Track Housing Element and RHNA Goals

Jurisdictions use the process of preparing the APR to track the implementation of their Housing Element and progress toward meeting their Regional Housing Needs Allocation (RHNA). When asked how their jurisdiction kept track of progress toward their RHNA goals, 47 survey respondents reported only using the APR. This indicates that dozens of jurisdictions rely primarily on the APR to take stock of local housing production. Beyond just meeting state reporting requirements, the APR enables local governments to fulfill a basic but essential function: tracking and measuring housing construction. As demonstrated by the following quote from a survey respondent, some jurisdictions may not be tracking their progress toward meeting their RHNA goals otherwise:

“If someone on the Planning Staff is tracking [progress toward meeting RHNA goals], I am unaware of it. We all have more than full time jobs just trying to keep our heads above water performing our everyday tasks.” (Small city in Bay Area)

Table B of the APR form compiles the jurisdiction’s RHNA goals by unit affordability level and approved units that count toward the RHNA goals, and calculates the remaining need. About 80% of respondents said that Table B of the APR is either “somewhat helpful” (31.8%) or “very helpful” (50.3%) for tracking their jurisdiction’s progress toward meeting their RHNA goals. However, multiple survey respondents reported that Table B’s usefulness is limited because it is difficult to update the information or correct mistakes from past years.
