Many jurisdictions use the Housing Element APR to track implementation of the programs and policy actions presented in their Housing Elements. About two-thirds of jurisdictions that completed the survey (65.3%) reported that they uncover updates about their Housing Element programs through the process of completing their APR every year. Notably, 63 respondents (36.4%) indicated that this is the only way they track program implementation. However, about half of jurisdictions (48.6%) said that they continually maintain a spreadsheet, document, or some other written source to track program implementation.

Taken altogether, these findings suggest that it is common for planners to rely heavily on retrospective data collection when preparing Table D of the APR.

3.3 Potential Interventions to Improve Data Collection

If HCD wants to hold jurisdictions accountable for inadequate APR submissions, the department should help set up local governments for success. Specifically, HCD should develop and provide assistance to local governments to help them track and manage housing development data that will be reported in the APR. Jurisdictions, especially those with less resources, would benefit from the additional support, and HCD could better equip jurisdictions to collect accurate data consistent with the department’s standards.

3.3.1 Interventions for Improving Primary Source Documentation

As described in this section, jurisdictions commonly face challenges linking project-level data across legal and development milestones when preparing Tables A and A2. HCD could provide assistance to jurisdictions to help them develop systems to link and track records across milestones, even when they are administered by different departments within a local government. The primary source documentation materials, through which jurisdictions process applications and issue approvals or permits, offer one intervention point for strengthening linkages between project-level data.

For jurisdictions that do not yet have this, HCD might work with the staff to set up a system where every project has a global unique identifier that is generated when an application is received and then attached to the project until its completion, which would make it easier for local government staff to track projects over time. Relatedly, HCD could provide guidance to jurisdictions on best practices for developing standard naming conventions to help link project data across development phases. Moreover, HCD could also support jurisdictions’ primary source documentation of affordability data, particularly for deed-restricted units where affordability commitments are typically formalized prior to the issuance of the building permit (if not before). By incorporating these features into their primary source documentation across the project lifecycle, jurisdictions would be better positioned to continuously update their tracking systems with relevant APR information in real-time, as both legal and development milestones are administered.

To support jurisdictions, HCD could offer templates for primary source materials (e.g., sample application forms) that jurisdictions could modify and adapt to their unique context, thus easing the burden of form design on jurisdictions and providing a clear course of action for planners pursuing this kind of improvement.

3.3.2 Interventions for Data Collection Throughout the Reporting Year

3.3.2.a Improving Software for Synchronous Data Collection

As described in Section 3.1.2a, jurisdictions use various software providers for their permit tracking systems. Having identified some commonly used software providers in this report, HCD might consider coordinating with those providers to help jurisdictions customize their software and improve their synchronous data collection for APR preparation.

Software systems designed for permit tracking can be customized to varying degrees, from modifying what fields are included, to integration with other systems. One key theme that emerged from our interviews is the importance of setting up software systems to be most useful for the jurisdiction’s needs. More than half of respondents (54.3%) reported that their jurisdiction has changed how it collects or stores data, or what pieces of information it collects, as a result of or in response to the APR reporting process, form design, or documentation requirements. Moreover, in open-ended survey responses, 29 survey respondents reported that their jurisdictions have modified their permit tracking software to make it more compatible with preparing the APR, such as by adding new fields to track information they previously were not collecting or by creating new report templates. Some planners we interviewed told us they have advocated for new fields to be added to project pages, such as checkboxes corresponding to binary, “yes-no” questions on the APR form.

An interviewee from one midsize city described how they made the APR process easier by using the customizable aspects of EnerGov, the software system from Tyler Technologies that the city uses to track projects. Specifically, they have developed custom “templates” that export from EnerGov the specific data required for the APR. The data exported to a spreadsheet formula makes it easier for the building department to review the data for accuracy and easier for planning department staff to input the data into the APR submission form. This city has relied on a completely online permitting system, one particularly “tech-savvy” team member, and strong teamwork across departments throughout the data validation process.

We interviewed another planner who described how she made major changes to their software. The city has used permitting software since 2020, when it was quickly set up by the building department during COVID. The program was not originally designed for APR reporting and was not very helpful for planners. Last year, the planner modified the software programming herself to make it more aligned with the APR.

As long as the APR uses an Excel form, how jurisdictions transfer data from their permit software to a spreadsheet format will remain a significant part of the APR preparation process. Currently, jurisdictions must all individually prepare these templates and figure out the customization settings on their own, but HCD could ease the burden on local governments by working with frequently used software providers to design export templates that are conducive to preparing the APR. To ensure alignment with existing APR systems and continued support moving forward, it would be beneficial for internal HCD to facilitate this coordination if pursued, rather than hiring an external consultant to do so.

It is important to acknowledge that many local governments face financial limitations that preclude them from investing in upgrading their software or dedicating staff time to developing new systems. This is a place where state funding, like Local Early Action Planning (LEAP) grants, can be particularly impactful.68 A midsize city in Northern California described using LEAP funding to streamline APR reporting by modifying their software to create data reports similar to the APR form. When funding is available, HCD should continue to proactively notify jurisdictions about these opportunities, and should provide support in navigating the application process for these funds.

3.3.2.b Sharing Best Practices Around Periodic Interim Data Collection Practices

To facilitate strong APR data collection strategies, HCD could share best practices with jurisdictions so that other jurisdictions know what strategies might help reduce the burden of collecting and compiling the APR form at the start of each year. For example, HCD might consider recommending the local jurisdictions perform periodic data collection throughout the reporting year, using the APR form or other templates.

Ten survey respondents and three interviewees reported maintaining a set of Excel spreadsheets, separate from the APR form, that serve as a master log of all of the projects in the jurisdiction. Planners who maintain logs like this describe how it helps them transfer their data into the APR submission form, facilitates cross-department coordination, simplifies year-round data collection, and helps to keep track of multi-year projects. Staff we interviewed from two large cities similarly described having developed practices to gradually work on the APR over the course of the reporting year. According to these interviewees, this practice has the benefit of spreading out the APR workload and reducing the pressure on planners at the beginning of the new year.

Both of the previously mentioned cities told us they have processes for collecting housing development data for Tables A and A2 and program implementation for Table D. In one city, the planner who leads the APR described inputting project information into a master tracking spreadsheet that resembles the APR form on a monthly or quarterly basis, effectively spreading out the work required to “translate” data into the APR format. In the other city, we heard about how planners periodically reach out to the affordable housing developers with local projects to get updates on how many units have been completed, are being rented, etc.

Additionally, both cities described having monthly or quarterly meetings with departments that work on implementing the Housing Element. In these meetings, local government staff provide updates on the progress on Housing Element actions that will be reported in Table D. By touching base throughout the year, these meetings are viewed as having helped improve accountability and information flow, and also provide a forum for the planner to have everyone in the same room to fill out the tracking spreadsheet for Table D.

Some jurisdictions reported including consultants or staff from outside of the planning department directly on the teams preparing the APRs. Three of the survey respondents were themselves contract employees working on APRs, and one reported hiring a subcontractor for additional support preparing Table D. Five survey respondents reported hiring an outside consultant to prepare part or all of the APR, and one interviewee reported sending their draft APR to a consultant for final formatting and revisions. Three survey respondents reported staff from departments other than planning playing a role in preparing the APR, and two interviewees reported staff from departments other than planning leading preparation for parts of the APR. Other departments that took leading roles in preparing parts of the APR included housing, building, and community development.

In one jurisdiction, the planning staff developed an internal spreadsheet, formatted similarly to the APR submission form, for the building department to fill in over the course of the year. When the APR submission form changes, the planning staff add new fields or otherwise modify the spreadsheet. Information that the building department does not collect, such as rents and sales prices, are filled in later by the planning department.

One interviewee described how the spreadsheet has streamlined the work of preparing the APR and how they believed it saved time in the process. Although the planning staff could produce this information through the city’s permitting software, it would require multiple exports from their software system. They believed that this process lowers the burden on planners for reporting accurate information in their APR submissions because the building staff, who are directly involved in permitting approvals, are able to identify data errors in the process of completing the spreadsheet.

This system likely functions well because most residential projects in this relatively small town are single-family dwellings and thus go through ministerial review with limited interfacing with the planning department. However, jurisdictions of varying sizes and characteristics reported taking a similar approach by developing a master spreadsheet, or series of spreadsheets, with a similar format as the APR form so they can easily transfer the data into the real APR submission form later.

3.3.3 Interventions to Improve Affordability Data Collection for Non-Deed-Restricted Units

The two types of affordable housing units reported on in the APR—deed-restricted and non-deed restricted—have different challenges, in terms of collecting and reporting data. When tracking down missing data for deed-restricted units, planning department staff can usually contact staff in the local government’s housing department or housing authority to obtain information about unit affordability levels. A large city even makes it regular practice to obtain and review the housing department’s dataset of housing covenants.

It can be more complicated for non-deed-restricted affordable units. Collecting affordability data for non-deed-restricted units is inherently difficult prior to the construction’s completion, as rent levels remain responsive to market conditions that fluctuate throughout the development lifecycle. Because developers are not typically obligated to lock in or report final rent levels for these units to local governments, APR reporting for this category relies heavily on estimation. Given that such data is often derived from observable characteristics (such as unit size and market location), this raises the possibility that HCD could estimate these values centrally, or at least provide more in-depth resources and guidance to help jurisdictions easily make those estimations on their own.

While many jurisdictions in California can reasonably assume that any new, non-deed-restricted housing is affordable only to above moderate-income households, some smaller, more rural jurisdictions could potentially have new units on the market with rents or sales prices affordable to moderate-income households or below. Identifying non-deed-restricted (naturally occuring) affordable housing units for the APR is an additional burden on local government staff in the jurisdictions where that kind of housing exists. In order to provide accurate APR data and receive credit toward their lower-income or moderate-income RHNA goals, those jurisdictions may be obligated to do additional fact-finding, as compared to jurisdictions that can reasonably presume that all new non-deed-restricted units are affordable only to households with above-moderate incomes. These jurisdictions that have naturally occurring affordable housing have to either collect data on the costs or rents of those specific units or come up with an informed estimate.

HCD has made strides in this area by developing the affordability calculator, which helps planners quickly determine a unit’s affordability by income level. However, the affordability calculator requires jurisdictions to know the unit’s monthly rent or sales price, which is often the missing piece of information, especially at the application, planning approval, and building permit stages. It is typically more readily available at the construction’s completion, because the rent is more likely to have been listed publicly on the rental market.

In many jurisdictions, most non-deed-restricted affordable units are ADUs. Several jurisdictions mentioned conducting surveys of ADU owners to ask what they change in rent. These surveys seem to be a promising approach to collecting affordability information for ADUs, though are susceptible to non-response bias. In comparison to ABAG and SCAG’s region- or county-wide estimates of ADU affordability levels, surveys provide recent and more localized information. While the quality of these affordability surveys is no doubt variable (and potentially subject to non-response bias), they may be effective for collecting data on constructed ADUs. Our study did not dig into the details of surveys or other methods of gathering data on non-deed-restricted affordable units, and this is a topic that would benefit from additional research to develop specific, actionable recommendations. HCD might consider evaluating the validity of local ADU surveys and consider issuing a standardized survey methodology to reduce non-response bias and ensure statewide consistency.

Further research would ideally focus on how jurisdictions currently collect data on housing affordability information and update it as a project moves through the development pipeline, and could identify jurisdictions with smart practices. Moreover, further study could identify viable validation strategies for ensuring that affordability levels reported at the permitting or construction completion stages actually correspond with the rents paid by tenants upon moving in.

Section 4: Data Entry and Verification for the APR

4.1 Perceived Ease of Preparing the APR Form

Local government staff reported and described challenges using the APR submission form in our survey and interviews. Our survey asked respondents how easy or difficult it is for them to “translate” the data the jurisdiction has collected into HCD’s APR submission forms. As displayed in Figure 15, almost half of survey respondents indicated that translating their data into the APR format was “very difficult” (19 respondents, 11.0%) or “somewhat difficult” (60 respondents, 34.7%), with only 3 respondents (1.7%) indicating that it’s “very easy.”

When asked in an open-ended survey question about the biggest challenges to submitting complete and accurate APR data, the most common response (given by 36 respondents, or 20.8% of the sample) was the form itself. In these open-ended responses, the APR tables were described as large and unwieldy, and respondents reported that deleting or correcting errors can be particularly difficult because of restrictions built into the form. Relatedly, 45 survey respondents (26.0%) recommended changes to the APR form’s formatting or design when asked for suggestions to improve the APR. In their written survey responses, seven planners described completing the tables in the APR form as “cumbersome.”

The level of difficulty planners experienced when preparing the APR is associated with their perceptions of the APR process and form. Of the 48 respondents who said translating their data into the APR format was either somewhat or very easy, 43 (89.6%) agreed that the APR process and form enables them to report accurate and complete data. Among the 79 respondents who instead said translating their data was somewhat or very difficult, the share of respondents who agreed that the APR process enables them to submit accurate data drops to 64.6% (51 respondents).69

Of the 89 respondents who said their jurisdiction’s information is mostly consolidated, 35 (39.3%) believe that translating their data to the APR is very or somewhat easy. In contrast, just 15.5% of respondents who reported their APR information is mostly in different places described data translation as easy.70

4.1.1 Specific Challenges Using the APR Form

In our survey, 28 respondents (16.1%) described challenges related to how the APR form’s programming and macros impose restrictions on users. In particular, planners commented that capabilities for copy-pasting by row are limited. Respondents from multiple jurisdictions reported that tables are too large to effectively navigate and that too many cells are locked. Two jurisdictions expressed concerns about automatic tabulations, including a concern that units in rows deleted from the form are still counted in totals. Although some of these limitations are addressed in the APR instructions and Frequently Asked Questions, the information does not appear to be fully understood by some local planning staff. Planners described their experiences using the APR form in their survey responses:

“[The] APR excel form is heavily locked to prevent edits. However, this format makes edits nearly impossible. Users are not even able to sort the form which makes editing and auditing difficult.” (Midsize city in San Joaquin Valley)

“[The biggest challenge is that] the macros create issues with copying the data. For example, the delete macros option does not remove the unit counts added in the line that is being deleted. They need to be cleared first and then deleted to show an accurate unit count. This required redoing the entire table to fix the additional units counted.” (Large city in Bay Area)

Seven survey respondents said that they believed the APR would be more manageable for planners if they had the ability to sort and filter the data, more easily “undo” mistakes, or “freeze” the top few rows in the Excel spreadsheet. This was corroborated by several planners we interviewed who reported that they had prepared the APR by first working on it in a copy of the APR submission form without the programmed restrictions, then transferred the data into the official submission form after it had been inputted, cleaned, and checked.

4.1.2 Difficulty Inputting Housing Development Data into Table A2

Interviewees reported that completing Table A2 (which collects data on planning approvals, building permits, and completed units) is particularly time consuming and labor intensive. This can be made more difficult, according to one interviewee, by the structure of the form: the large number of columns in the table make it so it can be hard or impossible for users to see every column at the same time. Consistent with these interviewees’ perspectives, 10 survey respondents specifically suggested reorganizing Tables A and/or A2 when responding to an open-ended question that asked how they would improve the APR.

Though the APR submission form has been constructed to include fields for all of the required information and intended to be suitable for most projects, interviewees felt that the current system is still not well-suited to reporting certain kinds of information. In particular, interviewees note that the current APR form is not set up to easily track large developments that begin with one large lot and result in hundreds or even thousands of new housing units. As described above, these “family-tree” developments can be more difficult to report in the APR, as compared to those that follow a more linear project pathway.

Likewise, a few interviewees reported that it can be difficult to document project amendments in the APR form. Some planners worried about incorrectly reporting units twice (“double-dipping”) or confusing the development timeline when they needed to report a project amendment (such as its number of units or the composition of units by income level) with respect to a development milestone that had already been reported in a previous APR.71 Relatedly, some respondents expressed a desire to amend the data in Table B. Three survey respondents reported that affordability information imported to Table B from past APRs is sometimes outdated and that errors are difficult to address because Table B is fixed.

Interviewees described how tracking a project as it moves through the development pipeline—by linking the project’s planning approvals, building permits, and construction completion—can create opportunities for errors or duplicates to emerge in Table A2. One survey respondent reported difficulty submitting projects with multiple building permits issued under a single entitlement, such as single-family subdivisions and multi-building residential projects. Another survey respondent expressed similar difficulty reporting large projects starting with a single entitlement, because the projects develop into multiple buildings with separate building permits. Focus group participants shared their difficulty linking building permits and entitlements for projects, because APNs, the common identifier, change over time. Compounding this challenge, projects often reach these milestones in different years and thus should appear in multiple years’ APRs, potentially making it more difficult to identify errors.

One large jurisdiction we spoke with described these kinds of challenges preparing their APR submissions. When their system was established about a decade ago, they were not yet required to link planning approvals and building permits in the APR, so they would collect the planning and building permit data separately. Now, they say they “spend a third of [their] time” in preparing the APR trying to link project data from different sources, such as by identifying which permits are connected with which planning approvals. A planner from this jurisdiction described the multi-hour process as “untangling things” and “investigating.” They suggested that the requirement to link planning approvals and building permits in Table A2 makes preparing the APR much more difficult than it was before that change. As two interviewees explained:

"About a third of our total energy in the APR process is somehow related to getting our own [individual] data into a format that HCD will take and accept. It goes far beyond a simple Excel template. We need to generate all this data of [planning approval] information and permit information... and putting it all together in one continuous chart. And tying that all back to a single line is very, very time-consuming." (Large jurisdiction in Southern California)

"It's a lot of work. Right now... for every one of those stages, I have to run a different report, and then I have to reconcile... it for Table A2. Because what I do... I have one project and show its progress through those different stages. I don't know if other jurisdictions just put the project in repeatedly with the different stages." (Large city in the Central Valley)

4.2 Practices and Challenges in Verifying Data

As described in Section 2.4, the majority of survey respondents in our study expressed varying levels of agreement regarding the extent to which the APR process and form structure enables accurate data reporting. Consequently, the planners working on the APR take steps to validate the data to ensure accuracy. Nearly ninety percent of survey respondents (89.6%) reported that their team performed audits of the APR data before submitting it to verify accuracy, identify duplicates, or check the data quality. Furthermore, 120 respondents (69.3%) said they reviewed other data sources or different systems to check the accuracy of their APR data, and, of these, nearly half said they checked more than one other source. One survey respondent described their jurisdiction’s process as such:

“To ensure data quality and accuracy we cross reference three different data sources. This includes building permit datasets, planning datasets, and housing covenant datasets. In addition, we include data screening steps at multiple steps of the process.” (Large jurisdiction in Southern California)

Validating data for the APR requires a significant amount of manual work, even if the jurisdiction has permit tracking software. Four survey respondents reported reviewing the APR line by line to find and remove duplicate entries. This review includes reviewing tables with hundreds of rows, such as Table A2. Five survey respondents reported asking staff involved in different parts of the permit process but outside of the APR preparation team to review the report for accuracy, including building officials, analysts, senior planners, planning directors, and outside consultants. Three survey respondents reported manually checking their APR data against individual permits. One planner said they felt this level of scrutiny was required to feel like the data was adequately reviewed. Another interviewee spoke to the capacity challenges of this type of data verification for large jurisdictions, where close to 100 planners are submitting permit data. This detailed review is time-consuming work that can be infeasible for jurisdictions with hundreds or thousands of entries.

As described in Section 2.1, larger jurisdictions spend significantly more of their time cleaning and verifying data, relative to other parts of the APR preparation process. Even so, planners from three large jurisdictions told us that they don't have sufficient time to do all of the data gathering, input, and manual validation that they would like to, and, because of that, they do find errors after submission. A key component of this stage in the APR process is identifying and eliminating duplicates, which, according to interviewees, can emerge, particularly in Table A2 when trying to link records for the same project over multiple years. Additionally, the same project might appear in the dataset multiple times if the address or APN changed. After the data has been inputted into the APR submission form, it can be hard to check if there are errors. The APR form excel template does not enable sorting or filtering, so there is no easy way to identify if a project has been repeated in the table, especially if that project’s APN has changed and/or there’s no unique identifier for the project. Moreover, it is unlikely that someone would notice if a project was missing.

Many people working on the APR utilize the built-in error validator tool, which identifies user errors such as empty cells that should be filled based on what the user has inputted. About two-thirds of jurisdictions (114 respondents, 65.9%) used the error validation function built into the APR form before submitting it for the 2024 report, and, in interviews, planners expressed appreciation for it. However, 27 survey respondents (15.6%) did not use it, and another 32 respondents (18.5%) were unsure or answered that they did not know what the error validator was. Additionally, two survey respondents reported using the error validation function, only for HCD to later flag additional errors in areas such as Table A2, columns AM and AO. Two survey respondents and two interview respondents also reported that the error validator is unhelpful because it identifies cells that it believes have an error but doesn’t explain what the error is. Multiple survey respondents reported that the validation function missed errors that were later identified by the staff member in a manual search. Some respondents suggested expanding the capabilities of the error validator to be able to flag duplicate addresses and APNs.

Part of the challenge in verifying APR data can stem from the weak connection between the planning and building departments, especially in large jurisdictions. In smaller jurisdictions, if the planners preparing the APR find something confusing or inconsistent or just have a question for another department, they often have the ability to, figuratively or literally, walk down the hallway to the other department’s office and consult them efficiently in person. In larger jurisdictions, it may be harder to get in touch with staff in other departments or to develop the kinds of relationships that enable collaboration. Sometimes planners must consult multiple documents to verify details about the project that have been collected and inputted into the APR form.

4.2.1 Verifying Affordability Data for Non-Deed-Restricted Units

While some jurisdictions ask for intended rent prices during the building permitting process, there is no way to be sure that those will not change by the time the construction is completed—or that the developer answered honestly about those prices in the first place. For completed units, some jurisdictions conduct surveys of developers and property owners to ask about sales prices or rental costs, though not all owners choose to respond. Eight of our survey respondents reported that their local governments collect this information from developers or property owners, with three respondents specifying that they conduct surveys of ADU owners to assess ADU affordability specifically.

Two planners we interviewed from a small, semi-rural jurisdiction said that property owners can be reluctant to share what they are charging for a rental unit with the local government. When that is the case, the planners then have to consult online resources or real estate market data to make an informed estimate of a unit’s rent and identify non-deed-restricted affordable units. Eight survey respondents reported relying on market data, such as current local rents of comparable properties, of which four specifically mentioned looking online on websites like Zillow and Realtor.com. Planners in a small city said that they search online for projects’ sales prices because the sales price is often so different from the project valuation that is collected to calculate building permit costs.

4.3 Potential Interventions to Improve Data Entry and Verification

4.3.1 Modifications to the Microsoft Excel APR submission form

4.3.1.a Change the programming of the APR submission form

One finding that arose from nearly all of our interviews and in many survey responses is that the Microsoft Excel APR submission form is challenging to use. When asked about the biggest challenges to submitting complete and accurate APR data, the most common response was the design of the APR submission form itself, which 21% of survey respondents mentioned unprompted.

Making changes to the APR form such as those described in section 4.1.1 is within HCD’s “form authority” and has the potential to save significant staff time.72 A revised form might lift some of the less necessary programmed limitations or macros. This change could limit frustration and reduce the amount of time planners spend working on data entry for the APR. One interviewee memorably described their experience “fighting with the macros.” Given the challenges reported, and acknowledging that APR form updates could require significant resources to accomplish, HCD might consider reassessing if the negative impacts of programmed elements outweigh the intended benefits. One survey respondent theorized:

“If the APR form was more user friendly and malleable, it would be easier to provide valuable information.” (Small city in Northern California)

According to study participants, planners could dedicate more time to reviewing the quality of their data if they were spending less time inputting data into the form. Planners from multiple jurisdictions described finding straightforward errors in the APR data they had already submitted and believed they would have identified those errors before submission if they had more time to perform data quality control.

Although planners experience challenges with the APR form, we acknowledge that HCD has taken measures to make the Microsoft Excel-based APR form easier for local government staff to complete. Specifically, the Microsoft Excel workbook is programmed to automatically run most calculations and to auto-populate some fields and tables. For example, Tables A, A2, and others include a “Summary Row” that displays an automatic count of the values in certain columns; these values are further consolidated in the workbook’s “Summary” tab. To clearly present the jurisdiction’s progress towards meeting its RHNA goals, Table B auto-populates with values drawn from the jurisdiction’s previous APR submissions once the jurisdiction name and year have been inputted on the “Start Here” tab. Additionally, throughout the workbook, there is optional conditional formatting to highlight cells that must be completed based on data the respondent has inputted elsewhere. These components of the workbook’s programming help ease the burden on the planners and may reduce the amount of time spent preparing the APR submission.

4.3.1.b Consider reorganizing Tables A and A2

As elaborated in Section 4.1.2, survey respondents, interviewees, and focus group participants described difficulties linking project-level data when completing Table A2 of the APR form, where jurisdictions report on planning approvals, building permits, and completed construction. Planners from large jurisdictions said linking this data was one of the most time-consuming and tedious parts of the APR.

Given this, HCD might consider alternative formats for collecting project-level data across legal and development milestones. For example, some planners suggested splitting Table A2’s three sections (planning approvals, building permits, completed construction) into different tables to make data entry more manageable. Splitting Table A2 into multiple tables could mitigate confusion among planners if project details change as it moves through the development pipeline. This could potentially reduce complexity and facilitate easier interdepartmental collaboration when preparing the APR, especially if different local departments oversee different milestones.

That being said, there are important drawbacks to consider when it comes to reorganizing fields and tables in the APR form. For projects that reach multiple milestones in the same year, planners preparing the APR would potentially have to re-enter certain pieces of information regarding the same project into multiple tables in a way that is duplicative. Keeping Table A2 together thus has advantages for projects with multiple milestones occurring in the same year.

Moreover, any pursued changes to the form should be designed and implemented with caution. The task of linking project-level data in Table A2 when preparing the APR form may be a way that jurisdictions notice when project information is missing across milestones. Reorganizing Tables A and A2 could have unanticipated consequences if the table configurations no longer facilitate verification of linkages between project-level data across milestones. If HCD seeks to move forward with this approach, they should only do so if there are sufficient resources to run a pilot with a few jurisdictions to substantiate its benefits before rolling it out to the whole state.

4.3.2 Consider changing the method by which HCD collects APR data

4.3.2.a Explore alternative web- or cloud-based APR submission models

In our study, 19 planners expressed a desire for a web- or cloud-based system to submit APR data more directly and easily.73 One planner opined that California, a state that creates cutting-edge technologies, should have a more sophisticated way to share housing data across government entities than Microsoft Excel spreadsheets.

Jurisdictions represented in our study have demonstrated a willingness to use new technologies to submit their APRs. HCD released a new Salesforce-based platform called HCD Connect, where jurisdictions could submit their APRs for the 2024 reporting year. Seventy-eight survey respondents (45.1%) reported that they submitted their APR using the new online submission platform. Of the respondents who used HCD Connect to submit their 2024 APR, 90.4% said it was very easy (41.1%) or somewhat easy (49.3%).74 Furthermore, only three respondents from jurisdictions using HCD Connect said that they or someone else on their team had previous experience with Salesforce before using HCD Connect, which potentially indicates that the planners working on the APR are capable of learning to use new technologies.

It is important to acknowledge that transitioning to a new web- or cloud-based APR platform could be a multi-year process that requires significant investment and coordination. Thus, this recommendation should be considered as a longer-term goal.

4.3.2.b Consider developing a submission model that retrieves APR data directly from permit tracking software

For purposes of streamlining APR data reporting, one potential approach would involve developing a system that automatically retrieves required APR data from jurisdictions’ permit tracking systems and transmits it to HCD. This idea was brought up by planners in our survey and interviews. To explore this approach, HCD might consider creating and piloting a streamlined submission method using an application programming interface (API) that integrates with multiple different permitting software programs to pull the APR data.

For example, a planner we interviewed drew a comparison between the APR and SolarAPP+, a platform used by many jurisdictions to automate solar permitting that can be integrated with a variety of permitting systems. SolarApp+ has designed an API that works with software such as Accela, Clariti, EnerGov, and Tyler EP&L that are also used for housing permits. All of these programs, commonly used by California jurisdictions, seem to run off of the same basic code, which suggests the state could set up an API similar to SolarAPP+ to automate or simplify the APR. The Data Strategy, an appendix to HCD’s 2022 Statewide Housing Plan, also discusses the potential benefits of an API for the APR submission.75

This strategy does have some potential drawbacks. Most obviously, there are California jurisdictions, including those represented in our study, that do not use permitting software. Moreover, further research is necessary to determine whether existing software, including the software identified in our study, could function with an API. Jurisdictions whose existing software are not compatible would potentially need to procure new software in order to benefit. Because it was commonly reported among study participants that multiple departments within local government use the same software for their various permit tracking needs, it stands to reason that changing systems would require inter-departmental coordination that could be challenging for some jurisdictions. Jurisdictions where this is infeasible would potentially have to submit the APR in a different way, perhaps with the same challenges and limitations they experience today. Even for the jurisdictions that could use the API submission method, HCD would likely need to develop new training materials for hundreds of planners across the state.

Another crucial limitation of this approach is that it assumes that the data entered by local staff into their jurisdiction’s permitting system is accurate. We learned from the survey and interviews that some jurisdictions review and clean their data during the process of preparing the APR. Having this kind of API-operated direct submission method could incentivize jurisdictions to do more regular data quality checks throughout the reporting year, but it could also result in lower-quality data being collected by HCD. It stands to reason, for example, that no one would notice a mis-typed address or that a project is incorrectly logged as utilizing a state streamlining law that it is not eligible for. Moreover, it is an open question how the system would respond if information required for the APR is missing from the jurisdiction’s permit tracking system.

Furthermore, while this method could work for reporting housing development data in Tables A and A2, local governments would probably have to work on reporting Housing Element program status updates in Table D separately. That information is typically not stored in the permitting software and providing accurate updates requires significant coordination with other local government entities.

Despite these unresolved questions and potential limitations, it would be worthwhile for HCD to further investigate the viability of an API-operated direct submission method for the many jurisdictions that could benefit from it. Understanding in more detail the functionality of SolarAPP+ and its potential applicability to housing data would be useful early steps, as would inquiring with permit tracking software companies that support this vision to understand what is feasible. Developing an alternative submission method should likewise be considered a longer-term goal and pursued with caution, so that the resulting transition is not hindered by inadequate resources or technical support on the part of HCD.

Section 5: HCD Communications

5.1 Instructions, Guidance, and Communications from HCD

In interviews, staff commonly reported relying on more experienced staff to help support them in learning how to complete the APR, particularly in their first year. In the focus group, two staff described relying on a more experienced coworker to show them how to complete the APR. That staff member was able to answer their colleagues' questions as they arose, based on their familiarity with previous APRs, what they had done in the past, and their previous communications with HCD.

Other planners we interviewed did not receive guidance from a colleague when assigned the APR and instead learned how to complete it using the instruction manual and resources prepared by HCD. Two interviewees expressed doubts that they completed the APR correctly in their first year assigned to it.

Our survey included several questions about whether and how respondents interacted with HCD staff while preparing their most recent APR. Ninety-seven respondents (56.1%) said they attended a webinar or attended an information session about the APR led by HCD staff, and 83 respondents (48.0%) said they sought help or technical assistance from HCD staff regarding the APR. About one-third of respondents (55 respondents, 31.8%) reported having attended an HCD webinar and also having sought help or TA, while 27.2% did neither.

Our findings suggest that jurisdictions are inclined to seek assistance from HCD when experiencing difficulty. Specifically, survey respondents reporting that it was somewhat or very difficult to translate their data into the APR format were more likely to seek technical assistance from HCD, as compared to those who reported it was not difficult. Among the 79 respondents who said it was somewhat or very difficult to translate their data into the APR format, 58.2% reported seeking technical assistance from HCD. In comparison, 47.9% of respondents who said translating their data was somewhat or very easy reported seeking technical assistance.76

Of the 125 survey respondents who attended a webinar or information session or who sought technical assistance, 87 respondents (69.6%) felt that HCD staff were able to answer their questions adequately.78 Jurisdictions reporting that it was somewhat or very difficult to translate their data into the APR format (as compared to those who reported it was not difficult) were more likely to seek technical assistance from HCD, suggesting jurisdictions are inclined to seek HCD assistance when experiencing difficulty. Among the 79 respondents who said it was somewhat or very difficult to translate their data into the APR format, 58.2% reported seeking technical assistance from HCD. In comparison, 47.9% of respondents who said translating their data was somewhat or very easy reported seeking technical assistance.79

Of the 125 survey respondents who attended a webinar or information session or who sought technical assistance, 87 respondents (69.6%) felt that HCD staff were able to answer their questions adequately.80 Figure 16 below (and Appendix Table E6) shows that most survey respondents (109 respondents, 63.0%) said that they were satisfied or very satisfied with the amount or frequency of communication from HCD to local governments about the Housing Element APR, and just eight respondents reported outright dissatisfaction (4.6%). Respondents were only slightly more critical of the clarity of communications from HCD: 98 respondents (56.6%) expressed satisfaction with the clarity of communication.

Some planners reported feeling that the instructions provided by HCD were limited and not always easy to understand. Four interviewees and two focus group participants shared suggestions to expand HCD’s instructional materials. In particular, one interviewee and one focus group participant requested online video explainers that they could reference when facing a roadblock, one interviewee requested a simpler way to schedule consultations with HCD staff, and one interviewee requested a specific onboarding process for staff preparing the APR for their first time.

Local government staff also reported making use of the APR instructions and seemed to find them helpful in explaining how to prepare the APR. Two survey respondents pointed out perceived discrepancies in the instructions about submitting the APR on HCD Connect, however, and one thought that certain definitions provided by HCD could be made clearer. Generally, these data suggest that the content of the instruction manual is not a primary barrier to reporting accurate APR data, and local planning staff seem to be comfortable reaching out to HCD when they need clarification on parts of the instructions. One survey respondent spoke positively of the APR instructions, while another was more critical:

“The terminology is clear. The APR instructions are a vital resource in helping us to complete the APR successfully.” (Midsize city in Bay Area)

“The emails sent from HCD Staff were very clear, and responses from them were prompt, including receipt of the updated APR. However, the requested corrections from APR Staff differed from the instructions provided in HCD's APR instructions published online. I was not able to find any more recently recorded webinar or memo on HCD’s website that laid out the reason these corrections were requested, which differed from previous years' requirements.” (Large county in Central Coast)

Another suggestion we heard from two focus group participants and one interviewee was that instructional materials from HCD should provide a deeper explanation of the purpose of the APR, and specifically how the data informs housing policy. Two additional survey respondents and an interviewee expressed confusion over why certain pieces of data are requested at all, such as planning approval and construction completion data if they are not counted towards RHNA goals.

Although the introduction to the APR instructions lists various statutes and bills that dictate the APR requirements, the planners with whom we spoke did not seem to sufficiently understand why they were being asked to provide all of the information required by the APR. Even among local government staff who reported believing it is important to collect housing data, many still wanted greater clarity on how specific pieces of information would help advance the state’s housing goals. This, they suggested, could make the work of preparing the APR feel less arbitrary and more meaningful.

5.2 Awareness and Communication of APR Form Updates

The planners we surveyed and interviewed generally reported being aware that the APR requirements change frequently, sometimes even annually. Nonetheless, most of the planners we spoke with during the focus group did not seem to understand why additional data is required by the state year-over-year. In addition to the focus group, six survey respondents and two interviewees also expressed frustration that they regularly have to update their data storage systems to stay up to date with shifting APR requirements, with one jurisdiction going as far as to say they have given up on updating their permit tracking software completely.

In the focus group and two interviews, planners suggested that, ideally, jurisdictions would be informed of any changes to the APR at least a year in advance, because they are collecting data required by the APR throughout the year. When the required APR tables change during or after the conclusion of the reporting year, it can interrupt data collection processes that happen year-round, and staff sometimes have to revert to manual data entry. Planners likewise noted that a standard annual issue date for the APR form would help them be more prepared. As one interviewee noted:

“What I understand from others is the APR data needs changes each year and that is one reason we have not updated our permit system to reflect and customize our data exports, because it changes each year with new information being requested.” (Small city in Northern California)

5.3 Potential Interventions to Improve HCD Communications

5.3.1 Provide Guidance to Clarify Common Points of Confusion

There are certain project types and unique situations that jurisdictions struggle to report in the APR and about which HCD could provide clarity. Specifically, planners communicated that it is not clear how they should report project amendments in the APR or precisely how to handle large master developments that ultimately have many housing units and multiple buildings, as previously described in Section 4.1.2. In both cases, planners seem to have rightfully concluded that the APR format was not set up with these circumstances in mind. HCD staff could issue guidance to jurisdictions about best practices for reporting on these kinds of circumstances in the APR.

5.3.2 Provide APR instructions and guidance in more and varied formats

The role of preparing the APR frequently shifts among local government staff members. As previously described, 20.8% of survey respondents reported that this was the first year they had prepared and submitted the APR. Planners we interviewed said they faced some difficulty when they first started working on the APR and relied on their colleagues with previous experience to help train them and answer their questions. While collaboration and learning from peers is generally positive—and is to be expected with a complicated task like the APR—support from colleagues should not be a necessary condition to succeed.

HCD’s APR Instructions and Frequently Asked Questions documents are helpful to local government staff but insufficient. By defining terms and explaining all fields in the submission form, the existing resources help users navigate the APR, which is unintuitive for many. That said, during the focus group, we heard from planners who identify as more visual or auditory learners that the written instructions are not the most useful to them and that they would benefit from instructions in the form of a video. Given this, we recommend that HCD develop and circulate one or more informational videos about the APR. These videos could provide context for the APR, describe any new changes to the form, and demonstrate parts of the APR preparation process using screen capture.

Similarly, participants recommended that HCD record its webinars related to the APR and post the videos online so that attendees can revisit the video to answer specific questions that arise and individuals who were unable to attend the webinar “live” can still access the content. Since we completed data collection for this study, HCD has recorded and posted a webinar for jurisdictions preparing the 2025 APR.81

Clarity in these videos, as well as the written instruction manual, is essential. As previously mentioned, just 56.6% of survey respondents said they were satisfied with the clarity of HCD’s communications—less than the percentage of respondents that were satisfied with the frequency of communications.

5.3.3 Communicate any new APR requirements at the start of the reporting year and provide technical assistance for implementation

Local governments are constantly generating data on applications, planning approvals, and building permits as projects move through the development pipeline. To the extent possible, this data is stored in jurisdictions’ permit tracking systems. As discussed in Section 3.3.2.a, more than half of survey respondents (53.3%) and multiple interviewees reported that they deliberately set up their software systems to be conducive for preparing the APR, such as by including fields to collect all of the required data.

When the APR changes from year to year, local governments must adapt to meet the new requirements. Even if the changes are relatively minor, it is possible that local governments have not been collecting data in that format or collecting that information at all. As described in Section 5.2, planners reported feeling frustrated when they become made aware of changes to the APR near the end of the reporting year, especially if the change requires them to track down pieces of information they had not been recording for projects because it wasn’t expected in prior years’ APRs. A late adjustment to the APR creates more work for local government staff in the few months before the APR is due, which is already a period of overwork for many of the people tasked with preparing APRs.82

It would be advantageous if jurisdictions were informed of any changes to the APR at least a year in advance so they can appropriately adjust their data collection and storage throughout the reporting year. As an example, this might entail modifying their application forms so project applicants submit certain pieces of information at the outset. This is especially challenging because making systematic changes can be a slow, gradual process, and local governments plan for them months or years in advance.

Although changes to the APR form and process are often statutory, to the extent possible, HCD should try to ensure that any changes do not go into effect for at least 1-2 years so that jurisdictions are given adequate notice of the change, especially if it entails collecting additional data. From conversations with HCD staff, it seems that this is already standard practice, as it takes time for HCD to implement legislation, and that this approach to implementing changes to the APR form will continue.

5.3.4 Clearly explain to local governments the goals and outcomes of the APR

Through the focus group, it became clear that there is a lack of awareness and understanding among planners about why every city and county in California is required to complete the APR. Comments from these planners suggested they view the APR as something HCD simply forces them to do, without realizing that the requirements come from statutes created by the California Legislature. This misunderstanding may lead some local staff to question the necessity of certain details — highlighting the importance of clear guidance to support consistent and confident reporting.

Furthermore, some planners in our study are not aware of what happens with the APR after they submit it to HCD. Many planners we interviewed were interested in knowing if and how the APR data influences the state’s programmatic or policy decisions more generally. Planners who are less aware of the APR’s goals and purposes may not view the APR as important to their work and thus be less intrinsically motivated to work on it. This is exemplified by the following quote from an interviewee:

“I don’t want us to have to [overextend ourselves to complete the APR on time] just because the law requires it. If there’s a purpose behind it, which I would think is to inform policy and policy changes, that’s not transparent to local jurisdictions.” (Large county in Southern California)

In all of its messaging about the APR, HCD should include a brief explanation of why local governments must collect and submit housing production data each year. This could include a brief overview of the history and goals of the APR at the beginning of videos and webinars about the APR, as well as in written instructions or guides to preparing the APR. HCD might also explain why the accuracy of specific data points is important for policymaking or evaluation, as this could help motivate planners to be diligent about checking data quality. Additionally, implementing this recommendation would require only a small amount of effort on the part of HCD and no additional burden on local governments.

Section 6: Discussion of Potential Interventions

Throughout this report, we have presented a range of interventions for HCD to consider that could potentially help address the challenges identified through our research. We position these options as alternatives to the status quo, with the status quo being the set of APR instructions, form configurations, and support services that HCD provided to jurisdictions for the 2024 reporting year.

While some alternatives are not necessarily mutually exclusive and could be implemented in combination, other alternatives represent distinct strategic paths, intervening at discrete points in the APR preparation process and potentially rendering other alternatives no longer relevant if implemented successfully. The present discussion is focused on mapping out these strategic paths and discerning how resource, capacity, and process differences across jurisdictions might render some interventions more or less applicable.

To map these strategic paths, we distinguish intervention alternatives in terms of:

  1. interventions whose effectiveness is potentially contingent on jurisdictional characteristics and circumstances (referred to as “potential interventions with dependencies”), and

  2. interventions that potentially have broad relevance to jurisdictions, regardless of their characteristics or circumstances (referred to as “potential interventions without dependencies”).

For interventions with dependencies, we’ve identified four dimensions of jurisdictional characteristics and circumstances that would conceivably influence the viability and feasibility of select alternatives for a given jurisdiction, including:

  1. the jurisdiction’s comprehensiveness of primary source documentation across legal and development milestones;

  2. the capabilities of the jurisdiction’s current permit tracking software, including its capacity for customization;

  3. the jurisdiction’s staffing and resource capacity; and

  4. the jurisdiction’s degree of governance fragmentation, specifically the extent to which the planning, building, and housing divisions operate separately or in coordination.

Potential interventions with dependencies include:

  • Interventions to improve primary source documentation

  • Interventions to improve retrospective and synchronous data collection

  • Interventions related to changing the APR submission method

Potential interventions without dependencies include:

  • Interventions to improve affordability data collection for non-deed-restricted units

  • Interventions to modify the programming or design of the APR form

  • Interventions to improve HCD communication methods and practices

These potential interventions without dependencies would address challenges we have identified as widespread and relevant to a diverse set of jurisdictions. HCD could consider implementing these interventions for all cities and counties, regardless of the jurisdictions’ human and technological resources.

For brevity, the discussion below focuses exclusively on interventions with dependencies, as those without dependencies have been sufficiently covered in the previous sections.

6.1 Potential Interventions with Dependencies

With over 500 jurisdictions preparing and submitting APRs each year, there is unlikely to be a one-size-fits-all solution to the challenges identified in this report. Interventions that could benefit some jurisdictions may have little impact in others, and jurisdictions may vary in their capacity to implement a given intervention in the first place due to staffing and funding limitations.

6.1.1 Interventions to Improve Primary Source Documentation

While jurisdictions vary on a number of factors, they share the common need for strong primary source documentation that ensures robust linkages between legal and development milestones. Some jurisdictions may already have strong documentation practices in place, where a housing project is assigned a unique project identifier at the application approval stage that follows the project to completion and where the number of units at different affordability levels are recorded across legal and development milestones alike.

For these jurisdictions, interventions for improving primary source documentation are irrelevant. For other jurisdictions, there’s potentially room for improvement and thus utility in receiving support from HCD along these lines. However, even among this latter set of jurisdictions, there may be further variation in jurisdictions’ degree of governance fragmentation that merits consideration. As previously mentioned, one potential intervention for HCD to consider includes providing improved templates for local application materials (e.g., housing applications and building permit applications) that a jurisdiction could incorporate into their documentation flow. If pursuing this kind of intervention, HCD should keep in mind these sources of variation among jurisdictions, and potentially develop a suite of application material templates that would be appropriate for different configurations of local governance. For example, HCD might provide one package that would be useful in jurisdictions where legal and development milestones are overseen by different departments, and another package that would be sufficient where the governance of legal and development milestones is less fragmented.

There are also capacity considerations when it comes to primary source documentation practices. The most comprehensive approach would entail robust documentation of both project identifiers and affordability data; however, between these two documentation targets, the project identifier is most critical. If a jurisdiction at least has robust documentation for unique project identifiers, then that jurisdiction could reliably trace development milestones (e.g., planning approvals, building permits, and construction completion) to legal milestones (e.g., planning- or financing-related deed restrictions). Even if documentation at some development milestones does not directly record affordability data, the logging of unique project identifiers across both development milestones and legal milestones would enable reliable linkages. For jurisdictions with limited capacity to overhaul their primary source documentation, a focused intervention to improve the documentation of project identifiers might be more appropriate.

6.1.2 Interventions to Improve Synchronous and Retrospective Data Collection

As described in this report, jurisdictions vary in their reported use of “gov tech” software for synchronous data collection and the extent to which they report that their software tracks the information required for the APR. For example, in response to an open-ended survey question, 36 respondents mentioned that their software does not track all data needed for the APR, and more than half of these specified that their software does not collect all affordability information. Additionally, 60% of survey respondents reported that their jurisdiction’s software does not track unit affordability for all permit types. For these jurisdictions, there are a few potential explanations at hand: (1) the jurisdiction’s software is not capable of comprehensively tracking these data even if re-configured, OR (2) the jurisdiction’s software is capable of this, but the jurisdiction has either (2a) not sufficiently tailored their software for the purposes of the APR and/or (2b) not incorporated adequate primary source documentation practices that enable comprehensive data entry into the software. When considering interventions related to software improvements, HCD should keep in mind these potential explanations and design interventions accordingly.

For jurisdictions with software that (1) is not capable of tracking certain pieces of data, it would be most beneficial for those jurisdictions to procure new software with more advanced capabilities; however, jurisdictions likely vary in their ability to do so. For jurisdictions with sufficient staff and resource capacity, HCD could provide guidance and advisory support to help facilitate the procurement and implementation of improved software. However, for jurisdictions without sufficient staff and resource capacity, it might be more appropriate for HCD to encourage those jurisdictions to adopt improved practices of periodic retrospective data collection throughout the reporting year. For example, HCD could encourage jurisdictions to engage in more periodic APR preparation throughout the year to reduce the burden leading up to the April 1 reporting deadline, with instructions that each local department that oversees a relevant legal or development milestone for APR reporting should participate. Given capacity constraints and governance configurations, jurisdictions using software with limited capabilities might be better off incorporating more frequent practices of retrospective data collection. For these jurisdictions, interventions by HCD related to coordinating software improvements are potentially less viable and, therefore, misaligned with local realities.

Notably, the set of considerations described in the previous paragraph would also apply for jurisdictions who do not use any “gov tech” software. For these jurisdictions, capacity constraints would determine which path is most appropriate — that is, either procuring capable software for synchronous data collection, or adopting improved periodic retrospective data collection practices.

In contrast, for jurisdictions with software that (2) is capable of tracking these data, the appropriate intervention depends on the specific bottleneck. HCD support should be tailored based on whether the jurisdiction primarily needs to customize its existing software (2a) and whether the jurisdiction also requires foundational improvements to its primary source documentation practices (2b). For the former, it would conceivably be sufficient for HCD to coordinate with relevant software providers to create standardized templates that would enable software customization for comprehensive affordability tracking. For the latter, HCD might consider a coordinated approach that accounts for factors described in Section 6.1.1, ensuring that documentation improvements are designed to align with the jurisdiction’s specific software parameters.

6.1.3 Interventions for Changing the APR Submission Method

The potential value of HCD changing the APR submission method is likely dependent on resolving observed challenges regarding on-the-ground data collection practices. As described in Section 4.3.2, some potential interventions within this domain include (1) exploring alternative web- or cloud-based submission models and (2) developing a submission model that retrieves APR data directly from permit tracking software. If pursued, these changes could meaningfully streamline the APR process across the board.

That being said, HCD should anticipate associated limitations, as low-capacity jurisdictions that lack capable software systems and have minimal ability to procure them would be unlikely to participate in an alternative submission model, especially one where an API enables direct digital transfer of APR data between software. While alternative methods for APR submission would not necessarily benefit jurisdictions with limited capacity for software improvements, HCD could still incorporate alternative methods, such that jurisdictions have multiple options for how they submit their APRs. Higher capacity jurisdictions could partake in an alternative submission model, while lower capacity jurisdictions could continue submitting via an APR form (which could be improved via interventions described in Section 4.3.1).

Importantly, if the data collection challenges observed in our study are not resolved, then the greater ease enabled by alternative methods for APR submission will only partially mitigate the level of burden placed on local jurisdictions to report accurate APR data. Consequently, HCD might consider pursuing this intervention strategy as a second-tier priority after facilitating improvements to jurisdictions’ primary source documentation and software systems. As described in Section 6.1.2, jurisdictions may vary in whether software improvements are the appropriate recourse, meaning that some jurisdictions (even after improving primary source documentation) will still rely on retrospective data collection practices using Excel. For jurisdictions where this is the case, changing the APR submission method would potentially have less applicability.

Conclusion

This study provides valuable insights about how California planning departments carry out a core responsibility. Preparing the Housing Element Annual Progress Report (APR) is a fulfillment of state requirements but also reflects the basic function of local government to keep track of what projects are being built and what permits are granted. Jurisdictions’ ability to complete the APR on time and at a high level of accuracy demonstrates local state capacity, as preparing the APR requires a well-trained staff, technological resources, and efficient practices.

The APR in its current form is still relatively new, and it is reasonable to assume the state will continue to collect data on housing production for years to come. As such, it is worthwhile for HCD to reflect on how it is working, to correct issues that are identified, and redirect course as appropriate. Our research provides HCD with insight into the experience of preparing the APR from the perspective of the local planners who oversee the process from start to finish.

This report sheds light on the challenges common across jurisdictions, as well as practices and processes jurisdictions have developed that work well for them. These effective practices include collecting most data for the APR synchronously with thorough primary source documentation and software systems, periodically collecting retrospective data for the APR over the course of the year (such as program updates for Table D), and configuring permitting software or other data storage systems to be conducive for preparing the APR. While local government staff are finding ways to make the APR easier, HCD should consider technological investments that would further streamline reporting or even make the APR obsolete.

For the state government as a whole, including the legislature, it might be worth taking a step back and asking if it is necessary to collect all of the data presently required by the APR. Relatedly, legislators and civil servants should explore if it is possible to collect pieces of information through methods other than the APR, rather than continue to add more and more questions to the APR.

This study also identified the need for additional research on a variety of topics. In some cases, new questions emerged through our data collection and analysis that require further research to fully address. Namely, how jurisdictions track housing unit affordability data surfaced as a particularly interesting topic deserving of more dedicated attention.
