Appendix B. Interview Protocol

Interview Protocol for Semi-Structured Interviews with Local Government Staff and Consultants

  1. Introduction

Facilitator(s) will briefly introduce the purpose of the interview and what participants can expect, touching on the key points below.

Thank you for taking the time to speak with us. We are researchers at the Possibility Lab at the University of California, Berkeley. We are collaborating with the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) to study how jurisdictions across California prepare their Housing Element Annual Progress Report (APR) submissions and what challenges they face.

Your participation is completely voluntary. You can choose to skip any question that you do not want to answer. Data will be aggregated and summarized in reports to HCD, and nothing you say will be specifically attributed to you.

This interview will last about an hour. Can we record our conversation for note-taking purposes?

Do you have any questions before we begin?

  1. Basic Information about the Interviewee(s)

Facilitator(s) will refer to the interviewee’s survey responses to inform this and following sections of the interview and to avoid redundancy.

B.1. What are your primary responsibilities in your role as a [job title]?

B.2. How long have you worked for this jurisdiction? Have you worked for any other jurisdiction or government entity?

B.3. How did you contribute to this jurisdiction’s APR submission this year? How many years have you worked on APR (for this jurisdiction or another)?

B.4. How did you get involved with/become responsible for preparing the APR this year?

  1. APR Process Description

C.1. Please walk me through your jurisdiction’s process of preparing its Housing Element APR from start to finish.

Potential Prompting Questions

  • Who is involved in the APR process and what are their roles? How do you coordinate and work together?

  • How would you describe your jurisdiction’s overall approach to completing the APR?

  • What system(s), including software, do you use to store data on projects and permits? Who inputs data into this system, and how? How does this software/dataframe “translate” to the APR form? Is it missing any information required by APR?

  • How long did it take to prepare your jurisdiction’s APR submission? How would you describe the level of effort you and your colleagues put into the APR this year?

  • Which tables are the easiest or most difficult for your jurisdiction to complete (other than Tables A and A2)?

  • Are there any tables in the APR form where the data remain mostly the same from year to year? If so, which ones?

  • How does your jurisdiction track housing element policy implementation for Table D?

  • How has your jurisdiction’s systems, processes, and/or capacity to prepare the APR changed in recent years, if at all?

  • [If they have worked on APR for multiple jurisdictions] How does this jurisdiction’s APR data and preparation processes differ from other jurisdictions where you have worked?

  1. Follow-up Questions Based on Survey Responses

These questions will be customized to the participant and jurisdiction, but they will likely touch on subjects such as staff capacity, data storage practices, lexicon/terminology used by the state and local governments, challenges completing the APR submission form, etc.

D.1. In the online survey you completed, we asked [Question X] and you answered [Response Y]. Could you expand on that? Could you clarify what you meant by that?

  1. Challenges

E.1. What do you think are the biggest barriers to submitting complete and accurate APR data?

E.2. Do you feel that you or your team has the capacity and resources to ensure the data you submit is complete and accurate, e.g., through deduplication, verifying against several sources, or other methods?

E.3. How confident are you that you fully understand what HCD is asking for in each field/column of the APR submission form?

E.4. Are there any factors unique to your local government, staff, or context that you believe might influence your jurisdiction’s APR submission(s)?

  1. Recommendations

F.1. How would you modify the APR process or forms to make it easier for local governments to complete?

F.2. How would you modify the APR process or forms to make the APR data a better source of information for the state on housing production and policy in your jurisdiction?

  1. HCD Enforcement

G.1. Next year, HCD plans to begin rejecting APR submissions they believe are incomplete or inaccurate and requiring that the jurisdiction submit a revised APR within 30 days. Were you aware HCD had this enforcement authority? How do you feel about this forthcoming change?

G.2. If your jurisdiction’s APR were to be sent back to you for revisions, how do you think you would respond? Do you believe your jurisdiction would be capable of re-submitting a revised APR within 30 days?

Appendix C. Focus Group Protocol

Protocol for Semi-Structured Focus Group with Local Government Staff

  1. Introduction

Facilitator(s) will briefly introduce the purpose of the focus group and what participants can expect, touching on the key points below.

[Possibility Lab staff on the call introduce themselves]

Thank you for taking the time to speak with us. We are researchers at the Possibility Lab at UC Berkeley. As you might remember from when we last spoke, we are collaborating with the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) to study how jurisdictions across California prepare their Housing Element Annual Progress Report (APR) submissions and what challenges they face. The goal is to develop recommendations for how HCD can improve the APR process and collect more accurate housing data. In addition to collecting information for our study, we hope that this group discussion will give you all an opportunity to share and learn from each other.

Your participation is completely voluntary. You can choose to skip any question that you do not want to answer. Data will be aggregated and summarized in reports to HCD, and nothing you say will be specifically attributed to you. We ask that you not reveal to others who is in this room and what people say without their permission.

This focus group will last about an hour and a half. We plan to record our conversation for note-taking and analysis purposes. If someone doesn’t want to be recorded, we can pause the recording when they speak.

After the discussion, we plan to share notes with you all that include some of the tips or best practices we discuss today.

Do you have any questions before we begin?

  1. Participant Introductions

B.1. Could each of you briefly share your name, job title, and the jurisdiction where you work? And as an icebreaker, what's one word that comes to mind when you think of the APR?

  1. Process Comparison

We would like to discuss and compare the processes that you and your colleagues follow to prepare your jurisdictions’ APR submissions. We are going to walk through a few steps or elements of the APR preparation process that we heard about in the surveys and interviews that stood out to us as interesting or notable. I’m also going to highlight some jurisdictions’ processes and ideas we heard about during the interviews that stood out as potentially good models.

Let’s start by talking about how your jurisdictions record data on housing approvals and permits.

C.1. We heard from several of you that your jurisdictions have challenges collecting and tracking some pieces of data that are required on the APR, specifically the affordability (income) levels of affordable units and how subsidized housing projects are financed (and, less crucially, if the unit is owner-occupied or rented). Why do you think that is? [If present, mention that Jurisdiction A might have a system where they’re able to track this info.]

  • How have you and your colleagues tried to address these challenges?

  • Follow-up: Is there anything that has worked particularly well or poorly for your jurisdictions?

C.2. Another issue many of you mentioned is that gathering all of the data for the APR can be difficult and time consuming. One reason for this might be the process of exporting the data from your permit tracking software to prepare it for the APR, especially Tables A and A2.

Jurisdiction B seems to have some success pulling data from their software. [If in attendance, have Jurisdiction B staff describe what they do, how they came up with it, and if they think it’s successful.]

  • What is this part of the process like for everyone? What, if anything, would limit those jurisdictions from implementing a similar system?

C.3. We have learned from the survey and interviews that preparing the APR usually requires collaboration with other departments within the local government.

The staff from Jurisdiction C seem to have a good system of collaborating with their Building department. [Ask staff from Jurisdiction C to share about their process, how they came up with it, and if they think it’s successful. Jurisdiction D also talked about this.]

  • How big of a challenge or bottleneck is collaborating with other departments?

  • Follow-up: What practices have you adopted to help with gathering all of the data for the APR?

  1. Potential web-based APR form

D.1. Some respondents expressed interest in HCD developing a web-based form to submit APR data, and HCD is looking into what it would take to establish an online system. [Maybe direct to Jurisdiction E because they spoke about this.]

  • How do you all feel about that? If it existed, would you choose to use it?

  • What would an ideal system look like? What features would it have?

  • Do you have any concerns about changing the APR model to this?

  1. Capacity and Logistics

E.1. From the surveys and interviews, it seems like there is a lot of changeover in who is working on the APR. Staff are assigned to do the APR for just a couple of years, then the task gets passed to someone else. Would you say that’s true for your jurisdiction? [Potentially ask participants to gesture or raise their hands.] That means that there are constantly new staff across the state who need to learn how to do the APR.

  • In the first year/cycle you put together the APR for your jurisdiction, what resources did you consult? What resources were helpful to you?

  • Did you consult the APR instructions provided by HCD? How useful were they? Could they answer all of the questions you had?

  • How would you improve the instructions to be most useful for local govt staff in your positions?

  • What materials or resources could HCD provide to make it easier for local government staff to learn how to prepare the APR? What format(s) would be most helpful?

E.2. The APR form often changes a bit from year to year. HCD makes edits to the form some years when the legislature passes new laws.

  • How do you find out about these changes? When do you start thinking ahead to the APR/paying attention?

  • When would it be most advantageous to get info from HCD? How early? What formats?

E.3. From the survey, we know that most jurisdictions started working on the APR in January or February this year, but that might leave jurisdictions pressed for time. Some jurisdictions have started gathering and prepping the data for the APR form over the course of the year, including a couple here. [Ask Jurisdiction F and/or Jurisdiction G to describe how they prep data year-round.]

  • What does everyone think about this method? How else do jurisdictions manage the timeline of preparing the APR?

  • What prevents jurisdictions from meeting the April 1 deadline?

  1. Closing

F.1. Is there anything you’d like to add about the APR process in your jurisdiction that hasn’t been discussed yet? Or any final thoughts on how jurisdictions can support each other in this process?

Thank you all for your time and input this afternoon. If anyone has additional thoughts they would like to share, please send me (Emily) an email.

Appendix D. Description of Qualitative Data Collection and Analysis

All interviews and the focus group were led by a Possibility Lab researcher, and most also included a second member of the research team who took notes and occasionally asked follow-up questions. The interviews followed a semi-structured format. We asked many of the same questions in most or all interviews but allowed the conversations to flow freely and go beyond the topics of our prepared questions.

All interviews were recorded, with the permission of the interviewee, so we could later return to the recordings for analysis if some part of the conversation was not captured by our notes. After the interviews, we cleaned and compared the notes taken by the interviewer and other research staff, and in some cases, we also listened to the audio recording of the interview to enhance our memory and fill in any important information that was missed in the notes.

To analyze the interviews and focus group, two members of the research team conducted thematic coding of our notes. We developed a codebook to guide our qualitative analysis, track the key themes that appear in the data, and organize our data by topic. The codebook was created and refined through a process that was both deductive - drawing from our research questions and background knowledge - and inductive - based on patterns observed in the data.

The codebook contains 14 high-level codes including:

  1. Training, onboarding, and instructions;

  2. Inter-departmental coordination;

  3. Workload and costs;

  4. Data collection/data entry;

  5. Data cleaning and validating;

  6. Data quality, accuracy, and completeness;

  7. Local governments reforming their processes;

  8. HCD's updates to APR form;

  9. Web-based APR form;

  10. Permit software and technology;

  11. Terminology;

  12. APR enforcement/accountability;

  13. Recommendations; and

  14. Other challenges.

  42. Results are based on a series of linear regression models using jurisdictions with fewer than 20,000 residents as the reference group. Compared to smaller jurisdictions, larger jurisdictions spent significantly more time cleaning data (F(3,169)=4.97, p<0.01) and verifying data (F(3,169)=3.14, p<0.05), and spent significantly less time collecting data (F(3,169)=3.96, p<0.01) and inputting data (F(3,169)=4, p<0.01). While only marginally significant, the model indicates that larger jurisdictions also tend to have spent more time coordinating within local government (F(3,169)=2.65, p=0.05). No statistically significant relationship was found between jurisdiction size and time spent coordinating with HCD or completing “Other” tasks (p>0.10).

  44. This total reflects responses from two survey questions. The first question—Do you work as an external consultant who prepared the Housing Element Annual Progress Report (APR) on behalf of this jurisdiction?—received 18 “yes” responses. The second question—Did your jurisdiction hire an external consultant to help prepare its 2024 APR submission?—received an additional 4 “yes” responses. These responses indicate a total of 22 survey respondents representing jurisdictions that worked with a consultant. Among survey respondents who personally identified as consultants, there were three cases where the survey respondent reported a job title of “contract planner” (i.e., a planner who works for the jurisdiction on a part-time basis).

  46. Interestingly, large shares of survey respondents reported contributions from the building department (77.5%) and also from the planning department (75.1%), even though planners are primarily responsible for actually preparing and submitting the APR.   47. A Fisher’s exact test indicates that there is a statistically significant relationship between jurisdiction population and the average number of hours the jurisdiction reports working on the APR each week (p<0.01).

    ↩

  48. These estimates are based on responses to two survey questions: “In which month did you and your team begin to prepare this year’s housing element APR?” and “When working on the APR, about how many hours per week, on average, did you and your team spend working on it, collectively?” We assumed that each month has four weeks and that respondents, on average, started the APR in the middle of the month. The response options for the number of hours per week were ranges, and we assigned each jurisdiction the value in the middle of the range they selected as their average hours per week (e.g., 4 hours for a range of 3-5 hours). We multiplied these two values for all jurisdictions to roughly calculate the estimated total hours spent working on the APR.

    ↩

  49. A linear regression indicates a significant association between jurisdiction population size and estimated total hours spent on the APR (F(3,154)= 6.83, p<0.01). Larger jurisdictions spend more time working on the APR each year, on average. Jurisdictions with more than 100,000 residents spend an estimated median of 80 total hours on the APR—double the estimated 40 total hours spent by jurisdictions with fewer than 20,000 residents.
